articles.body:
Migrating an existing MongoDB application shouldn’t mean starting over. The application code, data models, APIs, and integrations you’ve already built represent years of investment. The challenge is moving forward while preserving what works.

For many organizations, modernization is about more than moving a database to the cloud. It’s an opportunity to simplify operations, optimize costs, build on open-source technologies, and prepare applications for new requirements, including AI-powered experiences.

Azure DocumentDB provides a path forward. Microsoft’s fully managed, MongoDB-compatible database service is built on the open-source DocumentDB project governed by the Linux Foundation. It supports familiar MongoDB drivers, APIs, and tools while providing the benefits of managed Azure infrastructure.

But a successful migration requires more than copying data. It starts with understanding your applications, assessing compatibility, choosing the right migration approach, and validating your workloads before production cutover.

Our new eBook, Modernizing MongoDB-Compatible Applications: A guide to migrating workloads on Azure DocumentDB , explores the broader modernization opportunity and provides guidance for organizations planning their next steps.

Let’s look at how to turn that strategy into action.

Why modernize MongoDB applications on Azure DocumentDB?

Existing MongoDB applications often work well. What changes over time are the expectations placed on the platforms supporting them.

As application portfolios grow, organizations need consistent security and governance, predictable operational costs, and infrastructure that can scale with demand. Meanwhile, AI applications and agents increasingly depend on access to current operational data.

Azure DocumentDB addresses these needs through several capabilities:

Preserve existing investments: Continue using familiar MongoDB-compatible APIs, drivers, tools, and development patterns, while evaluating application-specific compatibility requirements.

Simplify operations: Reduce infrastructure management with a fully managed database service that supports independent compute and storage scaling.

Build on an open foundation: Use a service built on the open-source DocumentDB engine, based on PostgreSQL and governed by the Linux Foundation.

Prepare for AI: Store operational documents and vector embeddings together to support semantic search, recommendations, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and AI agents that need access to relevant, up-to-date business data and agent memory.

Extend with Microsoft Cloud services: Connect applications with Microsoft Entra ID, Azure Monitor, Microsoft Foundry, and Microsoft Fabric for security, monitoring, AI, and analytics scenarios.

The goal isn’t simply to move existing workloads. It’s to establish a data platform that supports today’s applications while creating opportunities for future innovation.

Start with discovery and assessment

One of the most important lessons in database modernization is that compatibility should be evaluated before migration, not assumed.

While Azure DocumentDB supports familiar MongoDB APIs and drivers, applications may depend on specific commands, aggregation pipeline stages, indexes, or other behaviors that require changes.

A practical migration begins by understanding which applications are running, how they depend on their databases, and what changes may be necessary.

Assess your MongoDB portfolio with Azure Migrate

For organizations operating MongoDB databases on-premises, Azure Migrate provides discovery and assessment capabilities to help plan migrations to Azure DocumentDB.

The MongoDB assessment experience, currently in public preview, helps teams evaluate discovered MongoDB instances, assess readiness, and obtain recommendations for target Azure DocumentDB configurations and estimated monthly costs.

This enables architects and IT teams to prioritize workloads, understand potential migration challenges, and build a phased modernization roadmap rather than moving every application simultaneously.

Learn how to assess MongoDB workloads using Azure Migrate.

Evaluate application compatibility with the Azure DocumentDB Migration Extension

Once you’ve identified a migration candidate, the Azure DocumentDB Migration Extension for Visual Studio Code provides a more detailed technical assessment.

Developers can analyze MongoDB feature usage, commands, query syntax, indexes, and configuration compatibility to identify potential issues before migration.

The assessment generates findings and recommendations at the database and collection levels, helping teams understand what can move as-is and what may require remediation.

Together, Azure Migrate and the Azure DocumentDB Migration Extension help connect portfolio-level planning with application-level migration readiness.

Explore Azure DocumentDB migration readiness assessment.

articles.title: Delivering Skills in NuGet packages
articles.feed_summary: Agent skills were introduced by Anthropic in 2025 and have quickly become commonplace for AI-driven development. dotnet/skills and Impeccable skills are
articles.body:
Agent skills were introduced by Anthropic in 2025 and have quickly become commonplace for AI-driven development. dotnet/skills and Impeccable skills are good examples. Agent skills are typically distributed via git repos. We’ve been working on skill delivery via NuGet packages and found that the approach can be effective. The common thread is that repos and packages are units of development that can be used as distribution vehicles for skills.

Skills solve two main problems: fill in gaps in model knowledge and can prescribe “our way” of approaching a task. New NuGet packages will always be ahead of model training and can benefit from just-in-time skill delivery.

Here’s a quick demo using the markout package, whch contains a set of skills:

$ dotnet-inspect package markout -S Skills
path size
skills/markout-built-in-shapes/SKILL.md 9457
skills/markout-composite-cells-cards/SKILL.md 6764
skills/markout-conditional-composition/SKILL.md 4978
skills/markout-output-formats/SKILL.md 7744
skills/markout/SKILL.md 8551

Baseline

We’ve done a lot of experimentation. We’ve found that agents (as a baseline behavior) are capable of finding content in the NuGet cache to learn about a package. This includes reading README.md files and even writing throwaway programs that reflect over assembly metadata. Agents using frontier models are impressively creative and can derive surpising insight, although not necessarily cheaply.

The fundamental question is whether they apply that creativity and capability to reverse-engineering documentation from metadata or working on your actual business problem. We sometimes say “why not both?”. It’s tough when you’re usage has to fit within a monthly token budget.

This is the problem we set out to solve.

SKILL.md

Skills are markdown files with a YAML header, named SKILL.md . agentskills.io is the official spec site for the format. NuGet-delivered skills use the same format.

The following example skill can be used to direct agents to run vulnerability checks on project dependencies.

---
name: vulnerable-nuget-package-check
description: Check a .NET project for vulnerable NuGet packages dependencies.
---

The .NET SDK includes a `dotnet package` command, which can list vulnerable direct or indirect package dependencies for a given .NET project.

Run the following command for a project:

```bash
dotnet package list --vulnerable --include-transitive

Update vulnerable package references to patched versions.

## Conventional delivery

Skills are distributed via git repos, in one of two ways.

The most common approach is to include skills in a typical "code" repo. This approach is a great starting point since everyone working on the repo gets the same experience. Skill composition changes with a PR workflow that the team can review or even revert. The [dotnet/runtime repo](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/tree/main/.github/skills) uses this approach. It is a great experience working on that repo and seeing a variety of skills automatically used by Copilot depending on prompts.

The other primary approach is skill [marketplace repos](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/customize-copilot/plugins-marketplace), such as [dotnet/skills](https://github.com/dotnet/skills). These repos advertise their skills via [marketplace.json](https://github.com/dotnet/skills/blob/main/.agents/plugins/marketplace.json). Users install the marketplace via `/plugin marketplace add dotnet/skills` (or similar). `add` is just a wrapper on `git clone`. That means a skill marketplace repo should be small.

The advantage of putting skills directly in your repo is that the skills are always there. A good example is using the [Copilot Web Agent](https://github.com/copilot). Locally installed marketplace skills don't exist off of your machine unless you take the extra step of committing them to your repo. Neither is better or worse, just different options.

## NuGet-package delivery

NuGet packages present a challenge and opportunity for agents. The challenge is that a new package version with new APIs published five minutes ago isn't part of the model. The opportunity is that updated skills can be co-located with updated binaries. That means that every version of a NuGet package can have perfectly-tailored skills for their use. It's very similar to package-resident `README.md` files, which are intended for a different purpose and consumer.

The challenge isn't limited to packages published in the last five minutes. Package registries also have a very long tail. It's quite likely models know nothing substantive about most packages.

`dotnet restore` already pulls packages to your machine to acquire libraries. That means that package-resident `SKILL.md` files will be on your machine as well.

You can see [markout](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Markout) package skills on my machine.

```bash
$ pwd
/Users/rich/git/dotnet-inspect/src/DotnetInspect.Cli
$ dotnet build
$ cat ../../artifacts/obj/dotnet-inspec

articles.body:
.NET Conf 2026 is just one week away! Join us November 10-13 for this free, four-day virtual conference and the official launch of .NET 11. We’ll kick things off with two days of sessions from Microsoft product teams, followed by two days of community-led talks from developers around the world.

Start at dot.net/conf for Microsoft’s sessions and conference information. You’ll find Community Days information on the community-run .NET Conf site .

Get ready for .NET Conf 2026

Four days of .NET

Here’s how the conference breaks down. All times below are Pacific Standard Time (PST, UTC-8).

Dates

What’s happening

Time

November 10-11

Microsoft product team days, including the .NET 11 launch

8 AM-5 PM PST each day

November 12-13

.NET Conf Community Days

8 AM-5 PM PST each day

You can browse the Microsoft session agenda and add sessions to your calendar. The agenda also lets you choose your time zone, so you can plan your viewing wherever you are.

Day one: .NET 11 launch

The conference starts on Tuesday, November 10, at 8 AM PST with Scott Hanselman and the .NET team. The opening keynote will explore what’s new in .NET 11 and how Copilot and agents fit into .NET development, including the applications you already have.

After the keynote, you’ll hear directly from the people building .NET. A few sessions to put on your calendar:

What’s new in C# with Mads Torgersen and Dustin Campbell, a look at what’s coming to the language.

Modern web development with ASP.NET Core & Blazor in .NET 11 with Daniel Roth, a demo-packed tour of the web stack.

What’s New in .NET MAUI in .NET 11 with Gerald Versluis, a practical tour of the latest improvements for mobile and desktop apps, testing, and the developer workflow.

The .NET AI Stack: What’s New, What’s Next, and How It Fits Together with Luis Quintanilla, practical guidance on choosing and combining .NET’s AI building blocks.

What’s New in Aspire for .NET Developers with Maddy Montaquila and Damian Edwards, a look at the Aspire and .NET developer workflow.

Beyond Autocomplete: Getting the Most from GitHub Copilot for .NET with Wendy Breiding, practical workflows for using Copilot throughout development.

The day also includes sessions on .NET MAUI, WinForms, the dotnet CLI, C# Dev Kit, security, and the .NET runtime. Check the full agenda for session descriptions and times.

Day two: Visual Studio and developer deep dives

Wednesday, November 11, starts at 8 AM PST with a Visual Studio keynote from Mads Kristensen. Join us for a look at the latest developer experiences and what’s coming next.

The day’s sessions include:

The State of AI in Visual Studio with Rachel Kang, followed by What’s new in Visual Studio with Jason Chlus.

What’s New in Visual Studio Debugging and Diagnostics with Harshada Hole.

What’s new in the MCP C# SDK with Stephen Halter.

Building the future of agentic UI with Blazor with Daniel Roth.

GitHub Copilot modernization with Mika Dumont, a walkthrough of a .NET upgrade.

Beyond Code Generation: Give AI Eyes and Hands for .NET MAUI with Gerald Versluis, demos of using GitHub Copilot with a running .NET MAUI app to inspect the UI, investigate problems, and verify changes.

There’s plenty more, including Windows app development and AI-assisted .NET MAUI workflows. Pick the sessions that match what you’re building, or try a topic you haven’t worked with yet.

November 12-13: Community Days

The conference continues with two full days of community-led sessions on Thursday and Friday, November 12-13 . This year, a community team led by Javier Lozano, working with members of the .NET Foundation board and other volunteers, is running Community Days, including session selection, hosting, and production.

Community Days are a chance to hear how other developers use .NET in their own projects and learn from their experiences. Visit dotnetconf.net for Community Days sessions, speakers, and viewing information.

Join your local community

Want to watch and talk about .NET with developers near you? The community site also lists local .NET Conf events, and you can organize your own .NET Conf event through January 15, 2027.

For now, save November 10 at 8 AM PST and head to dot.net/conf to plan your Microsoft sessions. We’ll see you at .NET Conf!

articles.title: Sparse Package
articles.feed_summary: We recently discussed External Location and how it lets Windows find files referenced in AppxManifest.xml but installed by some other (not-MSIX) installer. Many people call this kind of package a "Sparse package". Many even think sparse pack
articles.body:
We recently discussed External Location
and how it lets Windows find files referenced in AppxManifest.xml but installed by some other
(not-MSIX) installer.

Many people call this kind of package a “Sparse package”. Many even think sparse packages are the
important feature, and External Location is a minor implementation detail.

But…what is a sparse package?

First, let’s create one.

HOWTO create a sparse package

At its simplest, a sparse package contains AppxManifest.xml and other
footprint files ,
and no payload files. 1 For example, here’s a simple manifest for a HelloWorld application:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<Package
xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/appx/manifest/foundation/windows10"
xmlns:uap="http://schemas.microsoft.com/appx/manifest/uap/windows10"
xmlns:uap10="http://schemas.microsoft.com/appx/manifest/uap/windows10/10"
xmlns:rescap="http://schemas.microsoft.com/appx/manifest/foundation/windows10/restrictedcapabilities"
IgnorableNamespaces="uap uap10 rescap">

<Identity Name="HelloWorld"
Publisher="CN=Contoso LLC, O=Contoso LLC, L=Paris, C=France"
Version="1.2.3.4"
ProcessorArchitecture="x64" />

<Properties>
<uap10:AllowExternalContent>true</uap10:AllowExternalContent>
<DisplayName>Hello World!</DisplayName>
<PublisherDisplayName>Contoso</PublisherDisplayName>
<Logo>logo.png</Logo>
</Properties>

<Dependencies>
<TargetDeviceFamily Name="Windows.Universal" MinVersion="10.0.19041.0" MaxVersionTested="10.0.28000.0" />
</Dependencies>

<Applications>
<Application Id="app" Executable="helloworld.exe" uap10:TrustLevel="mediumIL" uap10:RuntimeBehavior="packagedClassicApp">
<uap:VisualElements DisplayName="Hello World!" Square150x150Logo="logo.png" Square44x44Logo="logo.png" Description="Say hello" BackgroundColor="#222222">
</uap:VisualElements>
</Application>
</Applications>

<Capabilities>
<rescap:Capability Name="runFullTrust" />
</Capabilities>
</Package>

The manifest declares <uap10:AllowExternalContent>true</uap10:AllowExternalContent> , indicating it
is intended for installation with an External Location.

Let’s create a PowerShell script to make a signed package with our manifest:

# Where to find inputs, a temporary workspace and save output
$sourcedir = 'C:\Projects\HelloWorld'
$workdir = "$env:TEMP\HelloWorldFiles"
$msix = 'C:\Projects\HelloWorld\Packages\HelloWorld.msix'
$cert = 'C:\Secrets\Contoso.pfx'

# Create the temporary workspace containing our input files
mkdir $workdir
copy "$sourcedir\AppxManifest.xml" $workdir
copy "$sourcedir\logo.png" $workdir

# Create and sign the package
makeappx.exe pack /o /h SHA256 /d $workdir /p $msix /nv
signtool.exe sign /fd SHA256 /f $cert /p "CertPasswordShhhDontTell" $msix

Notice the makeappx.exe command includes the /nv option. This command would normally fail as the
manifest references helloworld.exe but no such file is provided. The /nv parameter disables that
file existence check. This allows us to create a package without those payload files, such as
helloworld.exe .

Looking inside the .msix file via PowerShell…

$zip = [System.IO.Compression.ZipFile]::OpenRead($msix)
try {
$zip.Entries | Select-Object FullName
}
finally {
$zip.Dispose()
}

Shows us…

FullName
--------
logo.png
AppxManifest.xml
AppxBlockMap.xml
[Content_Types].xml
AppxSignature.p7x

This is effectively a signed manifest and logo with no helloworld.exe (as intended).

MakeAppx.exe
validates the contents, including that package-relative files referenced in AppxManifest.xml are
provided in the content directory ( /d parameter). Sparse packages are unusual because they
intentionally bypass that particular validation using /nv , allowing package-referenced payload to
exist only in the External Location.

Do I have to omit payload files?

No. You can continue including helloworld.exe and other payload files in your .msix as usual. But
Windows won’t use them.

Since Windows won’t use those files you can safely omit them and shrink your otherwise much larger
package down to a few KB.

So…why “sparse”?

When External Location was first described, this “install payload files via (whatever) installer and
omit them from the .msix” behavior was described as similar to
NTFS sparse files .
The file exists, but some of its contents wouldn’t be used, so that content can safely be omitted.
This makes the package rather tiny (usually a few KB) and simple to create.

But never underestimate the power of a catchy name.

People heard “it’s like a sparse package” and thought “Sparse package” was the feature.

It wasn’t.

External Location is the key feature. A sparse package is simply an optimization.

And not always desirable.

When to be less ‘sparse’

Earlier I mentioned you can include payload files in your .msix, but Windows won’t use them.

“Windows” being the operative word.

Payload files included in your .msix will be
staged in a new package directory
as usual, with the package’s footprint files – and with the usual
integrity protections and options .

Windows won’t lo

articles.title: Your app needs documents. Do you really want to build a document platform?
articles.feed_summary: File storage is rarely just file storage. Imagine your team is bui
articles.body:
File storage is rarely just file storage.

Imagine your team is building a contract management application. At first, the document requirement looks straightforward: upload a file, organize it, retrieve it, and let the right people open it.

Then the real requirements from your customer, security, and operations teams arrive, and the scope quickly expands to collaboration, authentication, permissions, governance, and administrative controls. What began as a feature has become a document platform. And now your team is spending cycles on content services instead of adding unique customer value.

SharePoint Embedded offers another path: your team builds the application’s user experience and business logic, while SharePoint Embedded supplies the underlying file and document management services. It is a cloud-based, API-only system built on Microsoft 365. Documents remain within the customer’s Microsoft 365 tenant and your application accesses them programmatically through Microsoft Graph.

The hidden scope behind “add documents”

A homegrown approach to adding documents to your app can look attractive when the first milestone is small. However, you’ll soon find that customers need granular permissions. Users will want to work together in Word, Excel, and PowerPoint without downloading copies or creating conflicts. They’ll also expect agentic experiences, fast search, previews, sharing, version history, and reliable recovery. Security teams will require audit, data loss prevention, retention, and eDiscovery. And then, Operations teams will need lifecycle controls, scale, and predictable administration.

The scope compounds to building and maintaining a document platform:

Content management: files, folders, metadata, search, versioning, recycle bin, restore, and lifecycle operations

Access: authentication, authorization, sharing, tenant isolation, and permission management

Collaboration: high-fidelity Office viewing and editing, co-authoring, AutoSave, and version history

Copilot and agentic experiences: ingestion, indexing, permission, and governance systems

Governance: auditing, retention, eDiscovery, and data loss prevention

Enterprise operations: scale, monitoring, administration, and integration with the customer’s Microsoft 365 environment

Every sprint your team spends recreating commodity content services is a sprint not spent improving the workflow, insight, or intelligence that makes your application valuable.

Add a document platform with SharePoint Embedded

articles.body:
Investigating an AKS incident, explaining an unexpected Azure bill, and connecting an agent to a knowledge base call for different expertise. With specialized Azure plugins, you can bring guidance for those tasks into your development workflow instead of assembling the context and procedures yourself.

The Azure plugin catalog now includes six specialized plugins alongside the core Azure plugin. They cover Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) operations, cost management, Azure Advisor recommendations, Kusto graph analysis, Azure Local, and Foundry IQ knowledge bases.

Use Azure plugins with the AI agent of your choice. In this post, we’ll explore what each plugin helps you do, share example prompts, and show you how to install the plugins you need.

Start with Azure, then add specialized skills

The core Azure plugin, called the azure plugin, connects your AI agent to Azure tools and skills for managing resources, deploying applications, and monitoring services. Additional plugins provide focused workflows for specific services and operational needs.

You don’t need to install every plugin. Add only the ones you need for your workflow to help manage your agent’s context window and leave more room for your code, conversations, and task-specific context. For example, add AKS Skills when troubleshooting clusters or Azure Cost when investigating spend, without bringing in unrelated capabilities.

The azure plugin also includes a discovery skill that helps you find these additional plugins as your tasks call for them. You can always install any plugin yourself, as described in the installation section below.

The following sections illustrate how specialized plugins complement the azure plugin across a range of Azure workflows.

Investigate AKS incidents with AKS Skills

When a Kubernetes workload fails, the useful evidence can span pods, nodes, networking, and Azure resources. AKS Skills ( aks-skills ) adds deeper operational guidance alongside the core Azure plugin’s cluster planning, setup, deployment, and baseline diagnostics.

Use it to investigate live incidents, match known error signatures to documented fixes, troubleshoot GPU and KAITO inference workloads, or collect bounded packet captures from selected nodes. Its cost-efficiency workflows also examine node scaling, workload placement, and Kubernetes-aware storage.

Try a prompt like:

Investigate why pods in my AKS cluster are stuck in Pending. Collect read-only evidence and explain the likely cause before suggesting changes.

Troubleshooting starts with evidence collection. Resource changes and packet captures require explicit approval. Install this plugin alongside azure plugin.

Understand and manage spend with Azure Cost

An unexpected bill raises several questions: What changed? Where is the spend coming from? What can we do about it?

Azure Cost ( azure-cost ) brings together four areas of cost management: analysis, estimation, optimization, and governance. Backed by the Azure Resource Manager MCP server, it supports investigating billed spend and anomalies, analyzing AKS costs, forecasting spend, estimating planned resources, evaluating commitment options, and working with budgets and cost guardrails.

If you used the cost analysis skill in the core Azure plugin, it has now moved into this standalone plugin. Install Azure Cost to keep using it.

Try a prompt like:

Investigate the increase in this subscription’s costs last month. Identify the main contributors and distinguish observed spend from any forecasts or estimates.

Turn recommendations into next steps with Azure Advisor

Finding a recommendation is only the beginning. You also need to understand which resources are affected and what remediation involves.

Azure Advisor ( azure-advisor ) helps you discover and summarize Advisor recommendations, identify resources affected by service retirements, and prepare remediation guidance for individual recommendations.

Try a prompt like:

Show the service-retirement recommendations affecting this subscription, identify the impacted resources, and explain the remediation guidance for one recommendation.

When Advisor doesn’t provide specific remediation guidance, the actionability workflow falls back to relevant public Microsoft Learn documentation. It identifies the source of the guidance and cites the documentation used, helping you distinguish Advisor-provided instructions from documentation-based next steps.

Explore relationships with Azure Kusto Graph Skills

Some investigations are about connections rather than individual records: how entities relate, which paths connect them, or how a suspicious activity chain develops.

Azure Kusto Graph Skills ( azure-kusto-graph-skills ) provides guidance for graph analysis in Azure Data Explorer. It covers Kusto Query Language (KQL) graph operators, including graph construction, pattern matching, shortest paths, connected components, and persistent graph models.

articles.title: How do you implement a random-access database when you don't have random-access external storage?
articles.feed_summary: The mystery comment investigated by Beej's Bit Bucket reminded me of a similar trick in an Apple ][ telephone directory program. The base Apple ][ was sold without a floppy drive. The only supported external s
articles.summary_zh: 文章回顾 Apple II 时代一个电话簿数据库程序如何在仅有磁带 I/O、无法程序化控制磁带启停与快进的条件下实现随机访问，程序用 BASIC 编写，数据存放在第 1000 行之前的注释块中。这是资源受限环境下巧用存储布局的经典案例。
articles.body:
The mystery comment investigated by Beej’s Bit Bucket reminded me of a similar trick in an Apple ][ telephone directory program.

The base Apple ][ was sold without a floppy drive. The only supported external storage device in the base unit was a cassette I/O port. Yet there was a database program for digitizing your phone list.¹ How did it do database stuff when the only I/O was a cassette drive? It could not programmatically start or stop the tape, or programmatically rewind or advance it.

If you took a listing of the program (which was written in BASIC), it began with a comment block saying not to edit any lines before line 1000. And then you saw your own telephone directory stored in DATA statements.² Followed by a bunch of dummy DATA statements. And then the program began.

Wait, how did your telephone directory show up as DATA statements? The BASIC DATA statement was a place for the program developer to store tables of precalculated read-only data, to be consumed by the READ statement at runtime. They shipped the program to you without your telephone directory in it, and yet somehow your telephone data ended up in the program.

That’s because the program used its own DATA statements as the memory for a database.

When it wanted to read from the database, it read the data via the usual READ command. And when it wanted to write to the database, it used self-modifying code to POKE the information back into its own DATA statements.

When you told the program that you wanted to save your changes, it told you to turn on the cassette player, and then it invoked the SAVE command to save the program to cassette. And since the program modified itself to contain your telephone data, saving the program also saved your data that was embedded inside it.

When you wanted to use your telephone directory, you loaded the program from cassette and ran it.

Now, the Apple ][ did have routines in the monitor ROM to save a block of memory to cassette, so it could have saved the database to tape in a more traditional manner. But that would have meant that when you wanted to use your telephone directory, you first had to load the program from cassette and run it, and then you had to set up the cassette a second time to load the database. Saving the entire program meant that the two load operations (loading the program and loading the data) were combined into a single cassette pass.

¹ This was back in the early days when the sales pitch for personal computers included “Organize your recipes!” and “Digitize your telephone directory!” Things that nobody ever actually did. (I don’t know how many people used it for personal finance, but it was definitely very popular for business finance .)

² At least, I think it was DATA statements. Maybe it was comments. But the same principle applies.

articles.title: Sneaking into the auditorium for the Windows 2000 launch rehearsal
articles.feed_summary: The Windows 2000 launch in San Francisco was accompanied by an expo, and a large number of Windows 2000 team members were dispatched to run the various booths and stations, give informal presentations on the new features of Windows 2000, and answer technical questions from the various attendees. And from among the people who were sent to th
articles.body:
The Windows 2000 launch in San Francisco was accompanied by an expo, and a large number of Windows 2000 team members were dispatched to run the various booths and stations, give informal presentations on the new features of Windows 2000, and answer technical questions from the various attendees. And from among the people who were sent to the expo, a smaller group was selected to attend the launch event itself in person.

Related reading : A ticket to the Windows 95 launch .

After a few of us arrived early at the Civic Auditorium for the launch event, we had to entertain ourselves until the doors opened. There was some speculation as to who the celebrity host would be, since it hadn’t been announced. One of my colleagues tried to sneak into what looked like a VIP tent.¹ I, on the other hand, went exploring.

I found an unlocked door that took me into the empty upper level of the main auditorium.

I took a seat and tried not to be noticed.

The stage was set up with a 10-meter tall mock laptop, screens to the left and right of the stage for projecting slides, prerecorded videos, or to get a better look at on-stage close-ups, gray curtains unobtrusively hung to shield from view what would turn out to be various surprises throughout the event, and various other desks, demo areas, and even an airplane cabin set.²

While I sat and took in the complexity of the stage, there was an announcement that they would be rehearsing the opening in one minute. The lights dimmed in preparation. The lid of the giant laptop closed very slowly .

About ten minutes after the announcement, the rehearsal actually began.

The laptop lid opened, and on the laptop screen, it looked like someone was signing into Windows 2000, and then the mouse clicked the Start button. This led to a video montage, and when the montage was over, a voice announced, “Ladies and Gentlemen, please welcome Patrick Stewart!”

Oh my goodness, Patrick Stewart is going to be the presenter for the Windows 2000 launch!

Mere seconds later, onto the stage bounded… a crew member wearing a headset pretending to be Patrick Stewart so that the camera and lighting crew could make sure they were properly positioned.

Okay, that’s the end of the rehearsal. The lights come back on, and the auditorium once again buzzes with the sound of equipment being moved and people discussing things.

I left the auditorium and went back to join the crowd of people waiting to get in. I didn’t tell them who the host was.

The event itself seemed to go off pretty much as planned. With the real Patrick Stewart.

Patrick Stewart had such a commanding presence. If he had come out on stage and announced, “It is the dawn of a new era: The era of lime Jell-O”, people would say, “Yeah, lime Jell-O, I need to upgrade to lime Jell-O.” But instead of trying to spark a new dessert trend, he talked about Windows 2000, reading words from a teleprompter that he almost certainly didn’t understand, but he made them sound great.

¹ My colleague eventually returned with a Commemorative Edition boxed copy of Windows 2000.

² The airplane cabin was used for a sketch that demonstrated mobile business computing. The demoer took their laptop on a plane trip, where they happened to sit next to a character named William Wentworth, portrayed by actor John O’Hurley, president of William Wentworth Worldwide. (He gave his email address as www@www.com .) The sketch demonstrated infrared file sharing and other mobile scenarios. Remember infrared file sharing? Of course you don’t.

articles.title: My Team Is Growing, How Do I Structure Who Gets Access to What?
articles.feed_summary: Your project started with one or two people. Now developers, operators, analysts, and applications all need access to Azure Cosmos DB. Giving everyone the same permissions might feel efficient, but it makes every identity more powerful than its job requires.
articles.body:
Your project started with one or two people. Now developers, operators, analysts, and applications all need access to Azure Cosmos DB. Giving everyone the same permissions might feel efficient, but it makes every identity more powerful than its job requires.

As your team grows, organize access around jobs, not people. Separate management access from data access, assign roles to groups and workload identities, and use the smallest practical scope. You do not need a complicated permission model for every person. You need a small set of repeatable access patterns.

This article is focused on Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL. Authentication and authorization options differ from other Azure Cosmos DB APIs.

Separate managing the account from using its data

Azure Cosmos DB access has two planes:

The control plane covers managing Azure resources: configuring the account, creating databases and containers, changing throughput, and managing role assignments. These permissions use Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC).

The data plane covers working with items: reading, querying, creating, updating, and deleting data. Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL provides its own native data-plane RBAC.

That distinction lets you separate jobs that are often combined. A platform engineer can manage account configuration without reading customer data. An application can read and write items without changing throughput or networking. Being an Azure Owner or Contributor does not automatically grant item access. Similarly, a Cosmos DB data role does not grant permission to configure the account.

Start with a small role model

Do not create a custom role for every team member. Start with the jobs your team actually performs.

Identity or group

What it needs

Starting point

Application developers

Build and test features

Data Contributor in nonproduction

Production application

Serve one workload

Managed identity with a scoped data role

Site reliability engineers

Diagnose health and configuration

Cosmos DB Operator; temporary data access if needed

Data analysts

Run approved read-only queries

Built-in Data Reader on reporting data

Platform engineers

Manage accounts, containers, and throughput

Cosmos DB Operator or a custom Azure role

The two built-in data roles cover many workloads:

If the identity needs to…

Start with…

Read items, run queries, and read the change feed

Cosmos DB Built-in Data Reader

Read, create, update, and delete items

Cosmos DB Built-in Data Contributor

Data contributor includes delete permission. If an application should write but never delete, create a custom data role with only the required actions.

For control-plane work, Cosmos DB operator is often safer than a broad contributor role. It can manage Azure Cosmos DB resources but prevents access to account keys and connection strings.

Use groups for people and managed identities for applications

Direct assignments to individual users become difficult to track as people join, change teams, and leave. Assign roles to Microsoft Entra security groups instead.

A group name should describe the service, environment, and responsibility:

cosmos-orders-dev-contributors cosmos-orders-prod-data-readers cosmos-orders-prod-operators

When a developer changes teams, you update group membership rather than searching for assignments across subscriptions and accounts.

Applications should not share those human access groups. Give each workload its own managed identity. An orders API might need Data Contributor on the orders container, while a reporting job needs Data Reader on a reporting database. Separate identities make both permissions and activity easier to understand.

Deployment automation should also use a different identity from the running application. Creating containers and processing items are different jobs.

Scope each assignment to the work

A data-plane role can be assigned at the account, database, or container level. Choose the smallest scope that lets the identity do its job.

For example, an application that processes orders can use Data Contributor on the orders container instead of the entire account. An analyst can use Data Reader on a reporting database without receiving access to operational data.

Keep environments separate. Development access should not silently become production access.

Environement

Useful human-access default

Development

Contributor access within the team’s resources

Test

Access required for deployment and testing

Production

No data access or read-only access, with elevation

Scope and role work together. A narrow role at account scope might still expose more data than necessary. A broad role at container scope might still allow actions the workload should not perform.

Make production elevation temporary

Production incidents sometimes require more access. That does not mean the access must be permanent.

Use Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management for eligible Azure RBAC assignments. For Cosmos

articles.title: How Microsoft SQL learned to recover without undoing everything first
articles.feed_summary: Under the Hood: The Research Behind Microsoft SQL, part 2 Here’s a scenario that used to be genuinely frightening: you kick off a bulk load of a few hundred million rows in a single transaction. Somewhere in th
articles.body:
Under the Hood: The Research Behind Microsoft SQL, part 2

Here’s a scenario that used to be genuinely frightening: you kick off a bulk load of a few hundred million rows in a single transaction. Somewhere in the middle, the server goes down. Not because of your load, just an unlucky reboot.

When SQL Server comes back, it has to undo everything that transaction did before anyone can touch those tables. Row by row (I think I’ve heard probably Bob Ward say “row by agonizing row” to describe this). Working backwards through the log.

That exact thing happened to an Azure SQL customer, and the team wrote it into the opening of their paper:

“Unexpected failure occurred while one of our customers was attempting to load hundreds of millions of rows in a single transaction. The database required 12 hours to recover while the corresponding tables were completely inaccessible.”

Twelve hours. The paper is Constant Time Recovery in Azure SQL Database (VLDB 2019), and it explains how recovery stopped depending on how much work your transaction did.

Why recovery was slow

Databases have used a recovery algorithm called ARIES since the early 90s (I did not know that before this paper, it stands for “Algorithms for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics”). I’m no expert, but I understand it runs three phases: analysis, redo, then undo. The undo phase is the problem. As the paper puts it:

“Recovering the database to a consistent state requires undoing all operations performed by uncommitted transactions which makes the cost of recovery proportional to the work performed by these transactions.”

Cost proportional to work done, yikes. A transaction that touched 50 million rows generates 50 million units of undo. On a departmental server in 1995, transactions were small (so I’m told – I was definitely not doing anything with a departmental server in 1995!). In a cloud service running millions of databases, where hardware fails and maintenance restarts happen constantly, that proportionality becomes an availability problem.

The idea: stop undoing, start ignoring

SQL Server already had a version store for snapshot isolation, where updating a row keeps the old version around in tempdb so readers see a consistent picture. This has been a topic that is always fuzzy for me, but the paper helped me understand. The innovation of Constant Time Recovery, or CTR, takes that and makes it durable (i.e., not in tempdb).

The Persistent Version Store (PVS) keeps row versions in the database itself, so they survive a restart. Versions live in two places: small changes are stored in-row as a byte diff next to the current row, larger ones go to an off-row table. By the way, it’s pretty crazy that the database just does this for you. The more I learn about the engine, the more I am impressed.

Logical revert is the payoff. When a transaction aborts, the system doesn’t walk the log undoing changes. It marks the transaction ID as aborted in an in-memory hash table called the Aborted Transaction Map . Any query that later encounters a row version written by that transaction skips it and reads the previous version instead. The abort is effectively instant. Cleanup happens lazily (I still smile that this is a technical term) in the background.

“The database is fully available, releasing all locks, while row versions are lazily cleaned up in the background.”

The SLog handles the leftovers. A few operations can’t be versioned, like certain metadata changes and lock acquisitions. Those go into a small secondary log stream that can be redone and undone in constant time, because there are very few of them.

The design choice I appreciate most is that they didn’t rewrite the engine, they just got creative:

“CTR combines traditional ARIES with multi-version concurrency control to improve recovery time without having to fundamentally redesign the storage engine.”

The numbers

Recovery time, measured across production Azure SQL Database:

Percentile

Traditional

CTR

99.9th

68 s

60 s

99.99th

over 10 min

1.3 min

99.999th

over 1 hour

3 min

The tail is where this matters. At the 99.999th percentile, over an hour became three minutes. Rollback also benefits from this, making it incredibly fast.

Source: Figure 9 from Constant Time Recovery in Azure SQL Database (VLDB 2019).

There’s a second benefit that surprised me the first time I read it. Because aborted work no longer has to stay in the log for undo purposes, the log can be truncated aggressively even while a huge transaction is running:

Operation

Traditional log

CTR log

10M inserts

5,101 MB

99 MB

50M inserts

25,873 MB

185 MB

50M deletes

38,255 MB

147 MB

That 50 million row delete used 38 GB of log before. Now it uses 147 MB. If you’ve ever had a maintenance job fill the transaction log and take an application down, you understand why that row matters. Crazy.

The cost is real but bounded, at least at the time of the paper. On TPC-C, an update-heavy workload, throughput

articles.body:
Siri AI is now open to all developers

November 3, 2026

Starting today with the iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and visionOS 27.3 betas, a new Developer Preview enables any developer to integrate their app with Siri AI, giving businesses and developers new ways to reach and serve their customers.
Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri that is profoundly more capable, conversational, and personal, is designed to be deeply integrated into Apple’s operating systems and the apps people use every day, including the apps from our vast ecosystem of developers. Thousands of developers have already built integrations with Siri to let users ask for directions, manage a to-do list, send a message, or catch up on an audiobook. Siri AI is available in many languages, including English, French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish and will soon expand to support Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese. People around the world are turning to Siri AI to get things done every day, which means more customers can discover and use apps just by asking.
Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, onscreen awareness, natural language, and more. So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order. For complex requests, we’re also introducing skills to let you teach Siri AI how to combine several actions into a single experience. And Siri AI can now surface any entity in the Spotlight semantic index, not just the ones that fit an existing schema.
We started rolling out these new capabilities across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather, so users can do things like find a coffee shop they visited last week or archive files that haven’t been opened in over a year. There are many more actions available now as examples for you to reference. To see what you can do in each app, just ask Siri AI.
This developer beta offers a sneak peek at Siri AI app intents for developers. With this early Developer Preview, your app can work directly with Siri AI, giving you a first look at new ways to reach and serve your customers. This preview provides early access before first shipping to customers in a few months; and with submission to the App Store opening up in the spring, developers have time to explore, build, and help shape their experiences before launch. Try it out and share your feedback.
As you explore early, we will follow up with more details about the terms and usage policies for experiences enabled through Siri AI. More to share soon.
To learn more about the new APIs, how to use them, and how to evaluate your app’s experience with Siri AI, read new documentation . You can also connect with Apple engineers in Apple Intelligence Group Labs on November 4–5 to ask questions, get advice, and follow the discussion.
Sign up for November 4, 9–10 a.m. (PT)
Sign up for November 5, 6–7 p.m. (PT)

Siri AI is available in beta in iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, watchOS 27.3, and visionOS 27.3 and requires an Apple Intelligence-enabled device set to a supported language. It is available in English, French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. Some features may not be available in all regions or languages.

Siri AI is currently unavailable in the EU in iOS, iPadOS, and watchOS. Apple is working constructively with the EU in an attempt to find a path forward.

Siri AI is not available for users under 13.

Certain Apple Intelligence features that rely on server-side models are subject to daily usage limits, including but not limited to Siri AI, intelligent photo editing tools, Image Playground, and AFM 3 Cloud models in Shortcuts. Daily limits may vary by feature, request complexity, system demand, system policies, and other factors. Expanded access to such features will be available for a fee in the future. Use of these features is subject to the Apple Intelligence terms and conditions. Learn more at support.apple.com/148587.

articles.feed_summary:

He digs the acoustic display enough that he can imagine Apple bringing it to a future high-end iPhone (like if they do a big redesign next year for the 20th anniversary), but he says you can feel the whole iPad shake if you turn the volume up high enough.

I’ve gotten very used to horizontal tabs over the years, but a long time ago I was a devoted user of the Omni Group’s OmniWeb browser, of which one of my favorite features was its vertical tabs. articles.body:
iOS 27.3 Adds Vertical Tabs and Adaptive Dark Mode to Safari

Tuesday November 3, 2026 10:51 am PST by Juli Clover

With iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS Golden Gate 27.3, Apple is making major updates to Safari. The browser is getting a Vertical Tabs layout, which can be used instead of the standard horizontal tab bar. It's a change that pairs well with the iPhone Duo 's larger display, but it is available across iPhone, iPad , and Mac.

Vertical Tabs are located on the left side of the display and use icons by default to save space, but there is an option to make the tab bar wider to show website titles as well. Vertical Tabs work with both Topics and Tab Groups to keep things organized. Topics are created when automatic Apple Intelligence tab sorting is turned on in iOS 27 . Pinning tabs by dragging, quickly swapping between Tab Groups, and other features also continue to work.

The option to turn on Vertical Tabs is located in the Safari settings or in the View menu on Mac and iPad.

Apple is adding Adaptive Dark Mode for websites that don't have a dark mode design option by default. If you use Dark Mode and then browse to a website with a bright background color, Safari will offer an option to "Try" Adaptive Dark Mode.

After tapping Try, Safari renders a Dark Mode version of the page that makes the background darker, changes text contrast, inverts logos and graphics, recolors vector artwork, lifts raised surfaces, and rebalances layered shadows. Each website will be adapted based on what's needed to make it readable, so not every tweak is applied to every site. You can opt to turn Adaptive Dark Mode on for all sites or on a site-by-site basis after using it.

If a site has a native dark mode or has a dark design already, Adaptive Dark Mode won't activate. Developers can also add a tag that causes Safari to ignore Adaptive Dark Mode and show the website as the developer intended.

Along with these visual changes, Apple is adding new Siri AI actions. Siri can take action on tabs and windows, sorting, moving, closing, and arranging in Tab Groups. Siri also has control over web history, and you can ask it to clear your history for a particular site and for a set time period, such as the last 10 days.

Siri can already see what's on your screen, but soon, Siri will also be able to understand the full content of webpages, including non-active tabs and content not in view. You will be able to ask questions about information across websites, so if you have multiple tabs open when shopping for an item, Siri will be able to sort them by price or give you information on the product that you're looking at. Apple says the Siri awareness feature is coming, but it's not in the first beta.

The changes to Safari are available for developers starting today in the latest betas. An Apple Intelligence-capable device is required for the Siri features.

iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS Golden Gate 27.3 will launch this December after several rounds of beta testing to refine the new features.

Tech

News

The New York Times sues Brave web browser for AI scraping and bypassing paywalls
Brave has allegedly provided ‘stolen copyrighted content’ to many AI companies.﻿

Brave has allegedly provided ‘stolen copyrighted content’ to many AI companies.﻿

by Jay Peters
Nov 2, 2026, 5:51 PM UTC

Photo: NurPhoto via Getty Images

Jay Peters is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

The New York Times and a group of other publications have filed lawsuits against the company that makes the Brave web browser over alleged unlawful scraping to train AI and also letting users bypass their paywalls, as reported by Reuters .

According to a complaint filed by the New York Daily News , the Chicago Tribune , and the Orlando Sentinel , Brave Software has monetized its index of scraped websites by, in part, providing AI companies with paid access to “real-time online content from the Brave Index.” The AI companies then use that index to train their models, access content to “respond to specific user queries,” or both. Brave has allegedly provided “stolen copyrighted content” to “many” AI companies including Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere.

Brave also promotes “hundreds of top publishers” as being accessible through its “Paywall blocker” feature in its browser.

“Brave has never asked for the Publishers’ permission to access their websites, much less to copy the material and provide it to users or other AI companies,” the complaint says. “On the contrary, as noted above, Brave allows its users to bypass the Publishers’ paywalls without their consent, and has taken other steps that prevent the Publishers from blocking Brave’s access to the Publishers’ websites. Brave has never compensated the Publishers for the unlawful use, copying, and distribution of the Publishers’ copyrighted content.”

“While we believe in the ethical and responsible use and development of AI, Brave has flouted established copyright law and ignored repeated requests by The Times to stop its infringing conduct,” Graham James, an NYT spokesperson, says in a statement to The Verge . “We filed this lawsuit to hold Brave accountable for stealing our content to power its own products and to provide it to some of the most prominent and well resourced generative AI companies in the world.”

“AI giants are now desperate to avoid getting caught red-handed stealing news from publishers, so Brave Software is selling them a back door to the journalism they know they have no right to,” says Steven Lieberman, the attorney who filed the lawsuit on behalf of the other three publications. “Buying stolen goods secondhand doesn’t make them legitimate. Brave must be held responsible for laundering pirated reporting for the AI industry.”

Brave, Anthropic, Mistral, SpaceXSI, and Cohere didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment. “ The New York Times is overpaying its attorneys and underpaying its journalists. (Who could’ve easily identified the disinformation in this suit.)” says Jesse Dwyer, Perplexity’s chief communications officer.

Update, November 2nd : Clarified that one lawsuit was filed by New York Daily News , the Chicago Tribune , and the Orlando Sentinel , not the companies that run them. Also added a statement from the attorney who filed the lawsuit on behalf of those publications.

articles.title: Steve Jobs on His Final Quarterly Analyst Call: ‘We Think the Open Versus Closed Argument Is Just a Smokescreen’
articles.feed_summary:
After linking to it earlier today, I re-read Steve Jobs’s remarks from his last appearance on a quarterly analyst call. It’s a banger of a good read:

You know, even if Google were right, and the real issue is
“closed” versus “open,” it is worthwhile to remember that open
systems don’t always win. Take Microsoft’s “Plays For Sure” music
strategy, which used the PC model — which Android uses as well — of separating the software components from the hardware
components. Even Microsoft finally abandoned this “open” strategy
in favor of copying Apple’s integrated approach with their Zune
player, unfortunately leaving their OEMs empty-handed in the
process. Google flirted with this integrated approach with their
Nexus One phone.

In reality, we think the open versus closed argument is just a
smokescreen to try and hide the real issue, which is, “What’s best
for the customer — fragmented versus integrated?” We think
Android is very, very fragmented, and becoming more fragmented by
the day. And as you know, Apple strives for the integrated model
so that the user isn’t forced to be the systems integrator. We see
tremendous value at having Apple, rather than our users, be the
systems integrator. We think this a huge strength of our approach
compared to Google’s: when selling the users who want their
devices to just work, we believe that integrated will trump
fragmented every time.

Prescient.

[ Editor’s note: Steve Jobs
had a lot to say Monday during his
conference call with analysts following Apple’s announcement of
record earnings and sales . Here’s the Apple CEO in his own words. ]
Hi, everybody. As most of you know, I don’t usually participate in Apple earnings calls, since you’re all in such capable hands with Peter and Tim. But I just couldn’t help dropping by for our first 20-billion-dollar quarter. I’d like to chat about a few things, and then stay for the rest of the Q&A, if that’s all right.

First, let me discuss iPhone. We sold 14.1 million iPhones in the quarter, which represents a 91 percent unit growth over the year-ago quarter, and was well ahead of IDC’s latest published estimate of 64 percent growth for the global smartphone market in the September quarter. And it handily beats RIM’s 12.1 million BlackBerrys sold, in their most recent quarter ending in August.
We’ve now passed RIM. And I don’t see them catching up with us in the foreseeable future. They must move beyond their area of strength and comfort, into the unfamiliar territory of trying to become a software platform company. I think it’s going to be a challenge for them to create a competitive platform and to convince developers to create apps for yet a third software platform after iOS and Android. With 300,000 apps on Apple’s App Store, RIM has a high mountain ahead of them to climb.
Google
But what about Google? Last week, Eric Schmidt reiterated that they are activating 200,000 Android devices per day, and have around 90,000 apps in their app store. For comparison, Apple has activated around 275,000 iOS devices per day on average for the past 30 days, with a peak of almost 300,000 iOS devices per day on a few of those days. And Apple has 300,000 apps on its App Store.
Unfortunately, there is no solid data on how many Android phones are shipped each quarter. We hope that manufacturers will soon start reporting the number of Android handsets they ship each quarter, but today that just isn’t the case. Gartner reported that about 10 million Android phones were shipped in the June quarter, and we await to see if iPhone or Android was the winner in this most recent quarter.

Google loves to characterize Android as “open,” and iOS and iPhone as “closed”. We find this a bit disingenuous, and clouding the real difference between our two approaches. The first thing most of us think about when we hear the word “open” is Windows, which is available on a variety of devices. Unlike Windows, however, where most PCs have the same user interface and run the same apps, Android is very fragmented. Many Android OEMs, including the two largest, HTC and Motorola, install proprietary user interfaces to differentiate themselves from the commodity Android experience. The user’s left to figure it all out. Compare this with iPhone, where every handset works the same.
Twitter client [TweetDeck] recently launched their app for Android. They reported that they had to contend with more than a hundred different versions of Android software on 244 different handsets. The multiple hardware and software iterations present developers with a daunting challenge. Many Android apps work only on selected Android handsets, running selected Android versions. And this is for handsets that have been shipped less than 12 months ago! Compare this with iPhone, where there are two versions of the software, the current and the most recent predecessor, to test against.

In addition to Google’s own app marketplace, Amazon, Verizon, and Vodafone have all announced that they are creating their own app stores for Android. So there will be at least four app stores on Android, which customers must search among to find the app they want, and developers will need to work with to distribute their apps and get paid. This is gonna be a mess for both users and developers.
Contrast this with Apple’s integrated App Store, which offers users the easiest-to-use largest app store in the world, preloaded on every iPhone. Apple’s app store has over three times as many apps as Google’s marketplace, and offers developers one-stop shopping to get their apps to market easily, and get paid swiftly.

You know, even if Google were right, and the real issue is “closed” versus “open,” it is worthwhile to remember that open systems don’t always win. articles.title: Apple’s Analyst Calls Have Been Scripted for Decades
articles.feed_summary:
Bloomberg opinion columnist Dave Lee :

Apple investors and fans hoping to get an insight into the
philosophy of new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus on Monday
were left sorely disappointed. The 51-year-old’s first earnings
call was a timid affair, with Ternus taking cover behind a
carefully written script as analysts peppered him with questions.

This is stupid. I mean, it would have been fun if Ternus’s style on the analyst conference call had been loose and freewheeling. Just like it would have been fun if the questions from analysts hadn’t been mostly insipid and pointless. But nothing has changed here other than who the CEO is. Tim Cook’s quarter calls were snoozefests. Save those recordings and use them to help you sleep. And that’s exactly how Cook wanted them.

What Ternus should do is follow Steve Jobs’s lead, and skip these calls except when there’s something exceptional to address. Let CFO Kevan Parekh and COO Sabih Khan handle them, the way Jobs used to let Tim Cook and Apple’s then CFOs handle them. At one point in 2008 , Jobs had only appeared on three of the calls in 11 years. He then appeared on the call in October 2008 to address the global financial crisis, and again in October 2010 (one year before he died) to celebrate Apple’s first $20 billion quarter and to throw shade at Android, BlackBerry, and competing tablets. In the 14 years of Jobs’s 2.0 stint as CEO, he only appeared on five quarterly calls. That’s the way to do it. Show up only when you have something worth saying. Otherwise the message remains clear: steady as she goes.

Apple CEO John Ternus criticized for ‘scripted’ approach to first earnings call

Ben Lovejoy | Nov 3 2026 - 4:54 am PT

9 Comments

Investors didn’t seem overly happy about yesterday’s Apple earnings call despite the record results . That likely reflects the company’s cautious take on margins in the current quarter, but some have also criticized what they describe as a very “scripted” approach by new CEO John Ternus .

Bloomberg was the biggest critic, describing it as a “timid” performance that left analysts “sorely disappointed” …

Bloomberg’s Dave Lee didn’t hold back.

Apple investors and fans hoping to get an insight into the philosophy of new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus on Monday were left sorely disappointed. The 51-year-old’s first earnings call was a timid affair, with Ternus taking cover behind a carefully written script as analysts peppered him with questions.

Top comment by FalcoMcGregor

Liked by 21 people

Newly minted CEO plays it safe during his first high-stakes earnings call? Absolutely shocking! Seriously, what did Bloomberg expect?

View all comments

Lee acknowledged that the slump in pre-market trading will have been largely driven by Apple’s caution about rising expenses in the current quarter. The company said that memory costs were continuing to rise and that building out Siri AI data centers we’re going to add to the RAM bill. But he argued that Ternus missed an opportunity to talk up the company.

In front of Ternus on Monday night was a chance to counteract the gloom and doom by instilling in Wall Street the fundamentals of the Ternus Doctrine — what he sees Apple becoming under his tenure, the “product guy” taking the company to a new era of innovation. Instead, he spoke like a man glancing at the clock and wishing the minutes away.

Fortune’s Sebastian Herrera was less vocal but echoed some of the criticism.

Ternus fielded some questions but also delegated answers to Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh and Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan, who Apple said would participate in earnings calls moving forward, something the company hasn’t done for years. Ternus projected confidence on the call, but he appeared to stick mostly to scripted marketing points.

9to5Mac’s Take

It will of course take Ternus some time to develop his own style when it comes to all of the varied aspects of the role, including addressing analysts in earnings calls, but I thought he took a measured but optimistic approach. Given the famously reticent style of his predecessor, the criticism strikes me as rather odd.

What’s your take? Please share in the comments.

articles.title: Apple’s New iPhone Release Schedule Seems to Pay Off
articles.feed_summary:
Horace Dediu, tweeting yesterday on Apple’s results:

iPhone grew at 17% sales which is amazing considering they did not
launch the 18 or the Duo or the new Air in the quarter.

The Duo didn’t launch until October, which is Q1 (in Apple’s financial calendar). And the Air, last year, was not a big seller ( putting it lightly ). The big bet Apple made this year was postponing the regular iPhone 18 until the end of winter early next year. The pro models — Pro and Pro Max — combined sell more than the regular non-pro no-adjective iPhone each year, but the regular non-pro iPhone is Apple’s single best-selling iPhone model . The bet that Apple made is that those mainstream buyers don’t care if the regular iPhone 18 ships five or six months after the 18 Pros — and won’t care next year, or the year after that, or the year after that about this same schedule being followed by the iPhones 19, 20, 21, etc.

The other factor at play is that the just-reported quarter started in July, just after Apple raised prices on just about every major product it sells other than the iPhone . So it’s theoretically possible that this quarter’s sales were boosted by people buying year-old iPhone 17-generation models in anticipation of Apple raising prices with the new models in September (which is exactly what happened). But I don’t see how that can explain 17 percent growth in sales year-over-year. Some savvy enthusiasts definitely did this. I have heard from a few people who bought iPhone 17 Pros in August, concluding that they’d be better off saving money than spending more for an only incrementally better 18 Pro (which would no longer come in the all-time-great cosmic orange colorway). But general consumers don’t follow Apple that closely. There are around 1.6 billion iPhone users worldwide , and I bet at least an entire billion of them have no idea that Apple always holds an iPhone introduction event in early September.

articles.feed_summary:
My thanks to WorkOS for sponsoring last week at DF. An agent can’t click through a signup page built for humans, so give it something it can read instead. Publish an auth.md file and agents register themselves without ever touching a browser login, and the user never gets pulled out of what they were doing.

With WorkOS auth.md, enroll in the dashboard and AuthKit publishes the file. Agents read it, register, and get scoped, short-lived credentials you control.

articles.body:
auth.md

Become an identity provider

For platforms whose agents act on behalf of users.

Read the provider guide →

One-click enable with AuthKit

Turn on Agent Registration in the WorkOS Dashboard to enable auth.md.

Read the docs →

FAQs

What is auth.md? A Markdown file an application hosts at its domain — typically https://yourapp.com/auth.md — that tells agents how to register on behalf of a user. It includes which flows are supported, which scopes exist, and how to register for the service. See the file format .

How does an agent register a user with my app? The agent fetches your auth.md , picks a supported flow, and either presents a verified identity assertion (agent verified flow) or walks the user through a code-confirmation claim (user claimed flow). You stay in control of which flows you accept and what credentials get issued. Read the apps guide .

What's the difference between the agent verified and user claimed flows? Agent verified is agent-attested — the agent's identity provider vouches for the user, no human in the loop. User claimed needs no provider — the agent shows the user a code, they sign in and confirm it. Most apps support both and let the agent pick the right one. Agent verified · User claimed .

What credentials get issued to the agent? A scoped access token tied to the user — short-lived and revocable. It's issued over standard OAuth, so you reuse the API auth you already have.

Is auth.md a WorkOS only feature or an open protocol? It's open. WorkOS authors the protocol, but auth.md isn't tied to WorkOS infrastructure — it composes existing OAuth standards (Protected Resource Metadata, ID-JAG identity assertions) and any app can publish or any agent can read one with no WorkOS account required. See the protocol on GitHub .

articles.title: GM to Pay $220 Million After Betraying Their Own Drivers’ Privacy
articles.feed_summary:
Jonathan Stempel, reporting for Reuters:

General Motors will pay $220 million to settle ​allegations that
it illegally sold drivers’ private behavior and location data to
brokers, who then sold the information to insurers that used it to
set and sometimes increase rates.

The settlement, announced on Thursday, resolves claims by the
attorneys general of 35 US states and the District ​of Columbia
over the automaker’s Smart Driver program, which enrolled millions
of drivers ​between 2016 and its discontinuation in 2024. Other
regulators have also reviewed GM’s handling of driver data.

GM was accused of pitching Smart Driver to help ​people improve
their personal driving safety, only to violate drivers’ privacy by
reneging on its ​promise not to sell their data without
permission. Many people who signed up were also enrolled in GM’s
OnStar safety, navigation and diagnostic service.

Reuters’s milquetoast headline was “GM to Pay $220 Million to Settle Allegations It Violated Drivers’ Privacy”. They’re not mere allegations. They did it. They just betrayed their customers’ privacy to make a few quick bucks.

I’ve driven a few GM rentals in recent years, and I’d almost certainly never buy one of their cars just because they’re poorly-designed pieces of crap. But even if they made a decent car I wouldn’t buy it. They’re still seemingly digging in on the CarPlay thing , and they ratted out their own customers to insurance companies.

★

articles.title: Rolfe Winkler at The WSJ: ‘The Beleaguered Chip Sellers Getting Their Revenge on Apple’
articles.feed_summary:
Rolfe Winkler, in a crackerjack story for The Wall Street Journal (gift link):

Blevins, who left Apple in 2022, sometimes set up
back-to-back meetings with suppliers so that rival sales teams
might run into each other, stoking competitive tension. Sales
representatives learned to pack nutrition bars to sustain them
through negotiating sessions that Apple executives sometimes
pushed past midnight without a dinner break. Blevins’s bad-cop
reputation gave his staff leverage: They threatened to call him in
if contract terms weren’t to their liking.

One significant contract term allowed Apple to audit its
suppliers’ books. Flash makers typically had to designate Apple
as a “most favored customer,” which guaranteed that no other
buyer got a lower price, according to people familiar with the
agreements. Apple’s audits allowed it to verify that no one
paid less.

Apple caught Micron selling flash at cheaper prices to another
customer and won an arbitration settlement worth tens of millions
of dollars more than a decade ago, said people familiar with the
dispute. Apple audited its suppliers so often that Blevins
negotiated a volume discount with the auditor, Deloitte.

The whole story is a fascinating and entertaining read. But I don’t get the “revenge” angle in the headline. The biggest buyers can negotiate the best deals. Apple used to be the biggest buyer, by far, for flash memory chips. They negotiated, with hardball but above-the-board tactics, the best deals. Now, Apple isn’t the biggest buyer — the AI datacenter hyperscalers are. Apple no longer gets the best deals. But they’re still getting fair deals. Apple is still negotiating the best deals it can for itself. So where is the “revenge”? The pinch mostly isn’t being felt by Apple — it’s being felt by Apple’s customers, who now face significantly higher product prices .

I included “ mostly ” in the preceding sentence because Winkler, in collaboration with the research firm TechInsights , makes the case in the pie…

Title: The Little Book of Generative AI Foundations: An Intuitive Mathematical Primer

Authors: Tianhua Chen

View PDF
HTML (experimental)

Abstract: This book provides a compact, derivation-oriented introduction to the mathematical foundations of modern generative artificial intelligence. Rather than surveying every recent architecture or implementation detail, it develops a coherent route through the ideas connecting major families of generative models, from PCA, probabilistic PCA, variational autoencoders, and diffusion models to normalising flows, autoregressive factorisations, GANs, Wasserstein GANs, and energy-based models. The aim is to make the structure of generative modelling more accessible without removing the mathematical substance needed to understand how these models are derived and related. The book is intended as a foundation-building primer for mathematically curious researchers, practitioners, and students.

Revised preprint version, 195 pages. Added visual explanations throughout. Comments and corrections are welcome
