articles.body:
Introducing Adaptive Dark Mode

Nov 3, 2026

by Simon Fraser, Luming Yin, Lily Spiniolas, Joanne Pan, Veda Periwal and Jen Simmons

We’re excited to announce Adaptive Dark Mode in Safari 27.3 beta. When enabled by a user, Safari adapts light websites and presents them as dark.

In the spring of 2019, Safari 12.1 became the first browser to support dark mode on the web. A lot of people love using dark mode, but not every website has a dark version. Almost 40% of web page loads are from users in dark mode, and yet only 10% of page loads support it. If you love dark mode, you’ve probably hit a site that felt particularly bright . Adaptive Dark Mode is designed to close that gap, providing a consistent dark experience across the web.

You can try it today in Safari 27.3 beta. To enable, first make sure your system appearance is set to dark. Then browse to a website with a bright background. Safari will offer a preview of Adaptive Dark Mode. Tap ‘Try’.

For websites that signal support of dark mode with <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark"> in HTML or color-scheme: light dark in CSS, Adaptive Dark Mode does not change a thing. For the rest of the web, it quickly analyzes the page, looking at colors and estimating whether it’s predominantly light or dark. If the page generally has a dark background with light text, nothing is changed. When a page has a light appearance, Adaptive Dark Mode adapts the page to be dark.

How does Adaptive Dark Mode work?

At the core of Adaptive Dark Mode is the transformation of color. Sometimes colors are simply decorative, while other times they have semantic meaning. Adaptive Dark Mode determines when to invert colors so elements remain visible or when to leave colors unchanged.

While creating Adaptive Dark Mode, we developed a color matrix to invert the luminosity of colors while preserving hue. It’s used to make light backgrounds dark, and dark text light. When transforming text color, Adaptive Dark Mode aims for sufficient contrast as defined by the WCAG 4.5:1 contrast ratio . Light CSS gradients are also transformed to dark.

Adaptive Dark Mode makes careful judgments so transformed content looks good and stays usable: buttons have contrast against backgrounds, text is visible over images, and hover menus look clear.

It takes the same care with images. Most are left unchanged, preserving their integrity. But many icons and logos can lose contrast when the background color behind them is inverted. So Adaptive Dark Mode inspects SVG images and transforms colors when needed. For bitmap images, it analyzes the pixel histograms and inverts simple black-and-white logos.

Effects like masks and mix-blend-mode can create undesirable results on an element whose colors have been transformed, so in some cases Adaptive Dark Mode turns such effects off. Also, <canvas> content is left unchanged, since canvases contain a wide range of content that’s hard to predict.

It’s precisely because Adaptive Dark Mode is happening deep within the WebKit browser engine that we are able to find creative ways to solve the most complex challenges, apply the transformations with great speed and power efficiency, all while rigorously protecting user privacy.

Making your site work even better

In general, a web page will work well with Adaptive Dark Mode if it follows good modern web development practices.

If your site still uses older techniques, small updates can help. For logos and icons, swap bitmap images for SVG. Use solid or gradient colors in CSS instead of tiled background images. Replace image sprites with modern CSS for rounded corners, shadows, and button states. Create content images with transparent backgrounds instead of baking the page background color into the image. Add padding to containers to prevent crowding.

Perhaps you want a specific dark mode experience for a certain portion of the page. Apply color-scheme: light dark to the relevant element and add your own dark styles.

Building your own dark mode

For complete control over how your site looks in dark mode, add full support. It’s a terrific time to do so. It’s never been easier.

Here’s an example of a website in light mode (left) and with Adaptive Dark Mode applied (center). If the site creates a custom dark mode, it could look like the third version (right).

All the web technology needed to fully support dark mode is widely available today, including:

<meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark">

:root { color-scheme: light dark }

@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { }

<picture><source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)">

light-dark()

Newer CSS functions like color-mix() and contrast-color() , plus popular techniques for organizing design systems with CSS variables provide additional options and flexibility.

Be sure to declare dark mode support using the color-scheme meta tag in your HTML head and/or by setting the color-scheme property on :root or body in your CSS. Don’t wait to inject this informatio

articles.title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
articles.feed_summary:

Points: 503

# Comments: 155
articles.body:
Simon Willison’s Weblog

Newsletter

Sponsored by: Greptile — Your code reviewer uses Computer Use to catch bugs by opening your app and clicking through it. Now you can configure its test environment and define the key user journeys it tests. Try it for free

Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too

3rd November 2026

Yesterday’s hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a “blog post”, but it’s paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model—literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I’ve been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I’m delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well!

Weight-Space Programming

Here’s the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights:

Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.

All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming .

The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models.

spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use.

I’m going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two.

The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games—Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up , it’s an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question:

The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response.

The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs . The exp1_which_game folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games:

breakout/prompt.txt

freeway/prompt.txt

pacman/prompt.txt

pong/prompt.txt

I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others.

Trying it out with Qwen 3.8 27B and other models

The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My LLM tool has a -f/--fragment option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this:

llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/breakout/prompt.txt \
-m openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro

This example requires the llm-openrouter plugin installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here’s what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro , which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens.

But how about Qwen 3.8 27B ? That’s still my favorite model to run on my own laptop—it’s just 17GB (I use this version ) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025.

I fired up LM Studio , ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the llm-lmstudio plugin and ran this command:

LMSTUDIO_TIMEOUT=900 \
llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/pacman/prompt.txt \
-m lmstudio/qwen/qwen3.8-27b

(I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see this issue .)

After 46m 12s and 43,506

Copy link

Description

indicava

opened on Oct 25, 2026

Issue body actions

Is there an existing issue for this?

I have searched the tracker for existing similar issues and I know that duplicates will be closed

Describe the Issue

Opening Postman on my Mac was followed by unexpected changes to my coding agents: recurring MCP authentication warnings and Codex repeatedly routing API work through Postman skills. Investigation found a user-wide Postman plugin, a startup instruction hook, a remote MCP connection, a Claude Code plugin, and a separately installed Postman CLI.

I consider automatically changing unrelated coding agents and attempting to approve your own instruction hook a severe consent and trust-boundary problem. An API client should not make itself the default workflow in other tools simply because I opened it.

Evidence from this Mac

Postman desktop: 12.33.4. Codex Postman plugin: 1.1.0. Installed source revision: 6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49. Investigation: October 25, 2026.

1. Postman's own log explicitly records automatic installation

From ~/Library/Application Support/Postman/logs/main.log, lines 11562-11563, timestamp 2026-10-24T09:34:14.418Z (12:34 Jerusalem time):

PostmanAgentPluginService~install: script completed
{"source":"auto-existing-upgrade","results":["claude-code:installed","codex:installed"],"installer":"script"}

Main: autoInstall.plugin.existing-user finished
{"outcome":"installed","platform":"darwin","exposed":true,"signedIn":true,"flagTimedOut":false,"useScript":true,"installer":"script","scriptResults":"claude-code:installed,codex:installed"}

2. Codex's global user configuration was changed

Relevant sections of ~/.codex/config.toml:

[ marketplaces . postman ]
source_type = " git "
source = " https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin.git "

[ plugins . "postman@postman" ]
enabled = true

[ hooks . state . "postman@postman:hooks/codex-hooks . json:session_start:0:0" ]
trusted_hash = " sha256:b67ddd1ece328f5a6f9103ce011bb58adb8411daea644f284732cff85d15cbb3 "
trusted_content_hash = " sha256:f3d02e32c39b39feaca37aec2b9bdbd308b6a2b7b3f7d2c52a0060e69eb9c345 "

3. The hook tells the agent to route broad API work into Postman

The installed hooks/codex-hooks.json registers a SessionStart command with matcher startup|clear|compact. It prints hooks/session-start-context.md, including:

Before responding to any non-trivial API engineering task — designing, implementing, mocking, testing, monitoring, documenting, or deploying an API or Postman Flow — load the postman:api-engineer skill and follow it.

That explains the repeated Postman skill announcements. This instruction is much broader than a user explicitly asking to use Postman.

Source: https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin/blob/6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49/hooks/session-start-context.md

Hook registration: https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin/blob/6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49/hooks/codex-hooks.json

4. The installer explicitly attempts to approve its own hook

installer/src/hosts/codex.ts invokes approvePostmanHook(system) after installing the plugin. installer/src/hosts/codex-hooks.ts obtains the hook hash using hooks/list and calls config/batchWrite to upsert hooks.state with trusted_hash. The source comment says: "Approves only Postman's current hook after installation".

Source: https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin/blob/6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49/installer/src/hosts/codex-hooks.ts

Caller: https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin/blob/6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49/installer/src/hosts/codex.ts

The source establishes the approval attempt. The trust record alone does not prove who created that specific record, so I am not presenting it as proof of a particular user interaction.

5. The remote MCP was enabled without a working authenticated connection

mcp.codex.json points at https://mcp.postman.com/mcp . Codex logs contain:

MCP server startup failed server_name="postman"
... error: Auth required, when send initialize request

Source: https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin/blob/6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49/mcp.codex.json

6. The installation also affected Claude Code and installed a CLI

The Trump administration is trying to stop Utah from enforcing its gambling ban against Kalshi, making Utah the 10th state sued by the US government agency that regulates prediction markets.

Meanwhile, Utah Attorney General Derek Brown filed criminal charges in a state court against Kalshi and its founders on Wednesday. The attorney general’s office provided us with court filings listing charges against KalshiEX, LLC , Kalshi co-founder and CEO Tarek Mansour , and Kalshi co-founder and COO Luana Lopes Lara .

The company and two co-founders each face 13 felony charges and one misdemeanor for violating gambling laws. The charges are based on sports bets offered on Kalshi between September 13 and September 24. “The state did not issue arrest warrants for Monsour and Lopes Lara. Instead, they have been issued summons to respond to the charges in Third District Court in Salt Lake County,” The Salt Lake Tribune wrote .

The Utah News Dispatch quoted a Kalshi statement vowing to fight the charges. “This is a crazy overreach; Utah is clearly playing politics. We look forward to putting a stop to this in court, just like we did in Arizona,” the statement said, referring to similar charges the company beat in Arizona in May.

Utah, which prohibits gambling, filed a civil lawsuit against Kalshi in a state court last week. Utah’s lawsuit seeks an order prohibiting Kalshi from offering bets on sports, elections, politics, and other events.

“Kalshi runs an online casino in Utah and calls it a prediction market. That violates Utah law,” Utah Attorney General Derek Brown, a Republican, said last week. “Not only do our state laws ban gambling but Utah is one of only two states where gambling is also prohibited under the state constitution. For 130 years, Utah has been clear: gambling has no place here, and we will enforce our laws.”

Utah already defeated Kalshi in federal court after the prediction market filed a preemptive lawsuit that sought to prevent the state from enforcing its gambling laws. Now that Utah is moving ahead in its attempt to shut down Kalshi, it must defend against a lawsuit filed by the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).

Trump admin claims sole authority

The CFTC “has filed a lawsuit against Utah to block the state’s efforts to shut down CFTC-registered contract markets using state laws,” the commission said on Tuesday . “The lawsuit follows Utah’s decision to file civil enforcement actions in state court against CFTC-regulated markets and other businesses. Utah’s effort to restrict the functioning of CFTC-registered exchanges obstructs Congress’s decision to federally preempt state law.”

If Utah can shut down Kalshi, that could spell trouble for Kalshi’s chief prediction-market rival, Polymarket, and for sports betting sites like DraftKings and FanDuel. DraftKings and FanDuel advertise availability in all US states via a mix of products , including prediction-market platforms in states like Utah. Both are registered with the CFTC.

The Utah attorney general’s office declined to comment today on the CFTC lawsuit. The CFTC previously filed lawsuits against Arizona, Connecticut, Illinois, Kentucky, Minnesota, New Mexico, New York, Rhode Island, and Wisconsin. The federal agency also filed briefs supporting Kalshi in appeals court cases.

“Utah seeks to shut down prediction markets across a wide variety of markets,” CFTC Chairman Michael Selig said. “Event contracts do not just serve hedging and investment purposes—they also provide the public with information about the outcome of future events. Congress entrusted the CFTC to be the federal regulator with sole responsibility to oversee these markets. As I’ve said before, the CFTC has the expertise and responsibility to defend its exclusive jurisdiction over commodity derivatives, and that’s exactly what we’ll do.”

The US Commodity Exchange Act (CEA) gives the CFTC authority to regulate swaps. The key legal questions being grappled with by courts throughout the US are whether event contracts offered by prediction markets qualify as swaps, and whether the CFTC jurisdiction over swaps preempts states from applying their gambling laws.

US sues in same court where Utah beat Kalshi

The CFTC is suing Utah in the same US district court that previously ruled in Utah’s favor. Kalshi sued Utah in February in an attempt to stop the state from bringing an enforcement action against the prediction market.

In August, US District Judge Robert Shelby granted Utah’s motion for summary judgment and denied Kalshi’s motion for a preliminary injunction. Shelby wrote , “[T]he court concludes the federal law relied upon by Kalshi does not preempt Utah’s ability to enforce its anti-gambling laws.”

articles.body:
Chances are you’ve seen me on X : unpacking hundreds of MacBook Pros to deploy in a datacenter. The video hit a nerve: insane enough at the first sight, yet kind of rational if you know what we know now.

Namespace
@ namespacelabs

Unboxing Macs at scale for our new server racks.

4:27 PM · Aug 24, 2026 · 25M Views
1K 964 5K 1.8K

So today I want to give some background into what it takes to build custom Mac racks, how we can start macOS instances from scratch in seconds and deliver new Xcode versions mere hours after Apple releases them .

So why MacBooks?

Because our customers need Macs. And because Apple didn’t give us another option.

Many of our customers build and test iOS apps. You can't build iOS apps without a Mac. The iOS Simulator only runs on a Mac. Moreover, in order to release an app to the App Store, Apple requires using a recent Xcode version. xtool xtool is cool, but it is not (yet) a serious replacement. So your coding agent needs a Mac.

But still, why laptops? Isn’t it a major waste of screen pixels and keyboard buttons and battery ions? Well yes, Mac Mini would be a better choice for a datacenter. Sure, it has very rudimentary remote management, no redundant power, and a beautiful case that ensures that cooling will be difficult regardless of which side you lay it on. But these are all known challenges that we have learned to manage.

But have you actually tried to order a couple hundred Minis? We have. Ordered in January, delivered in July. Welcome to the world of 2026 when the supply chains are in disarray. Never mind that Apple doesn’t release updated CPU models to all devices at once. So Mac Mini didn’t get M5 cores for 10 months (and then suddenly got M6 before any other device model!). We promise the best and the newest to our customers so we had to be inventive. That’s how the MacBook-in-Datacenter project was born.

Our beautiful Mac racks

Good design takes iterations; and we surely didn’t get everything right from the first try. But I think we have the system nailed down.

Every MacBook is connected to an IP KVM for remote management. Indispensable when dealing with laptops. Unlike Mac Mini, laptop firmware is designed with the screen in mind: some maintenance actions can only be done by clicking buttons in the beautiful GUI.

Of course, every MacBook gets an external 10G Ethernet NIC. Many folks at Namespace are networking geeks and we are proud of the connection speed and reliability that we provide to customers.

And then there is power. So in total, four cables per laptop, forty-eight per shelf, plus twelve for Ethernet, plus KVM wiring. Let’s just say that careful cable management is essential.

Heat management too. Currently we are deploying custom-made holders, designed to wick the heat from the hotspots and guide hot air away instead of blowing it at the nearby machines.

Not the problems we expected: HDMI, FileVault, and USB NICs

Naturally, we expected problems and challenges. Just not where they appeared.

I bet some of you looked at the pic above, saw MagSafe cables plugged in and already started writing a snarky tweet that MagSafe is not safe and may get accidentally disconnected.

And yes, I was worried about that too. But the reality is that we have seen very few cases of MagSafe disconnections.

The most unreliable cable? HDMI! Often thick and inflexible. Tends to fall out every time you touch the shelf.

Luckily by now we found almost perfect cables that bend exactly as we want them to bend. And we bought the entire supply of them. There are zero more of them available to order on Amazon.

Another source of pain: FileVault disk encryption. Or rather decryption. When a MacBook reboots (in an unplanned fashion) it prompts for a password to unlock the local disk. The prompt is shown on the screen (of a closed laptop somewhere in the rack, doh). No problem, we thought: we have the KVM connected just for this case!

Nope, not so easy. The password prompt disappears from the external screen after 5 minutes of inactivity. Then we remembered that macOS Tahoe introduced a useful feature: we could unlock FileVault remotely using SSH protocol. Still no luck. On laptops it expires after 5 minutes too. Looks like the only way out of this state is to reboot by physically pressing the button and racing to unlock in time. Mac reboot While on this topic, a small tip: you can reboot a Mac in a way that will keep the disk unlocked when you need it: fdesetup authrestart .

And then there are simply bugs. Under certain conditions, an external USB NIC stops working and acts as if it is not powered and shows no link. Trying another cable, another NIC, another switch port, no luck. But a quick visit to Network Preferences, deleting and recreating the “network service” in MacOS Settings brings it back to life.

What about Mac Minis and Studios?

At the moment we actually have it easy: M5 and M6 Mac Minis and Studios are coming into our fleet soon. They are way simpler to manage in th

articles.title: The 'Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen' post is misleading
articles.feed_summary:
Article URL: https://honnibal.dev/blog/astra-read-write-misleading

Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50351111

Points: 914

# Comments: 192
articles.summary_zh: 文章质疑“Astra 能读写权重以改进 Qwen”的帖子，认为其多项实验像魔术表演一样用不同手法制造效果，从而误导读者对其原理的判断。
articles.body:
Stage magicians often do the same trick multiple ways.
One iteration uses a gimmick prop, the next one shows you the prop isn’t gimmick but that one palms the object, the third time was a forced choice etc.
When you watch the performance you assume there’s only one technique, so each time they do it they seem to debunk your hypothesis about how it
must be working.

This is pretty much how the experiments in the ‘Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen’ post work. The post’s abstract says:

Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.

If you read that, would you assume that the Qwen experiment worked ‘just by looking at the raw weights’? Well it doesn’t. There’s experiments that look at raw weights, and experiments that improve a game-playing network, and an experiment that improves Qwen at maths. But those latter two aren’t just working with raw weights, they write Python programs.

Here’s a summary of what the post actually does and how the techniques work.

¹ Given one recorded episode of the failure.

³ Weights start at zero, so there’s nothing to read.

⁴ Beats PPO-500M only on Breakout (517 vs. 25); loses to it on Seaquest (53 vs. 89) and Asterix (53 vs. 55).

⁵ Runs up to 16 texts and sees only the attention patterns, not the outputs.

The “just by looking at the raw weights” setting (raw floats in context, no tools, no
running the network) only appears in experiments 1, 2 and 4, on networks of 17K–172K
weights. Every experiment involving a real language model uses Python, and the
Qwen result, which is the headline one, also gets to run the model on up to 50 batches of practice problems.

What the Qwen result actually shows is that Astra can be prompted to devise and perform tasks that
a human ML engineer could do. Human ML engineers write snippets of code that analyse or
even modify network weights “directly” all the time. Figuring out how to do this productively is not
nothing, and AI models of a year or two ago would have failed at all these tasks.

But to me the Qwen result and the other experiments that use Python don’t belong in the same post or paper as the experiments that read the weights directly.
A single technique that could achieve both, “Author weights for a small game from scratch” and “Improve the performance of a large model on a sample task” would imply a deep capability. If you test a single technique that way you’ve demonstrated a sort of ‘gestalt’ of the weights (it can write them out from scratch) and also that it understands a large existing network. But that’s not at all true here, because it’s not a single technique.

articles.body:
Main

Papers

Talks

Code

Writing

Writing

Could a modern chess engine on a Pentium have defeated Kasparov in 1996?

by

Nicholas Carlini

2026-11-01

On February 10th, 1996, a computer program (IBM's Deep Blue)
defeated the reigning chess champion (Garry Kasparov) in a game of chess for the first time.
Deep Blue would go on to lose the match,
but a year later, would get its revenge in a 3.5-2.5 rematch.

In order to achieve this feat, IBM spent several million dollars on research and
development building a special-purpose computer specifically for this purpose.
Deep Blue itself (the victorious, upgraded version)
was powered by 30 P2SC processors each running at roughly 120 MHz,
and (most importantly) 480 custom VLSI chess co-processors used to perform chess-specific
operations like move generation and position evaluation.
When it was built, Deep Blue was the 259th most powerful supercomputer in the world,
and could analyze over 200 million chess positions per second.

But was Deep Blue necessary to beat Kasparov?
Or could we have gotten away with an off-the-shelf 1996 desktop
running a smarter chess engine?

As it turns out, we could easily have beaten Kasparov without building Deep Blue, using only commodity hardware,
and it (almost certainly) wouldn't have even been close.
I know this because, as I write this very sentence, I have sitting next to me a
200 MHz Intel Pentium Pro (released exactly 31 years ago---November 1st, 1995) with 64MB of RAM
running a custom port of Stockfish that plays at an estimated Elo of
3300 ± 87 at classical time controls---far beyond the strength of any human, or indeed Kasparov's Elo of just under 2800.
But wait, there's more! I've hooked this machine up to the internet with a Realtek RTL8139C Ethernet card,
so you can play it below!

copy link
Analyze on lichess

← All games

Connecting to the Pentium…

Resign

Other games in progress

Play vs. the Pentium

The Pentium Pro's monitor, live (its VGA text screen, refreshed every second)

wait, what?! how??

There are three ways to get stronger at chess: you can
analyze more moves, analyze better moves, or analyze moves better .
Famously, humans improve by doing the latter two:
the average chess grandmaster during a classical game will analyze roughly the same number
of moves as an amateur player, but they analyze only the most critical moves and
do a better job with that analysis.
Chess engines like Stockfish , running on silicon instead of our human brains,
dominate us at the first of these
and analyze millions of positions per second.
And because there's not that much room for micro-optimizations on modern engines that will let a given
CPU process more positions per second,
most progress in chess AI also tends to follow how humans improve and finds better methods
for selecting moves and analyzing boards.

Skill in chess is measured by an Elo score.
A difference of 200 Elo means that you should expect the stronger
player to win three out of every four games, and multiplicatively from there: a 400 Elo gap corresponds
to a 90% expected score and a 1000 Elo gap gives a 99.7% expected score.
The best chess engines that you could run on commodity 1996 hardware were rated roughly 2300 Elo.
Deep Blue was rated 2700.
In contrast, modern Stockfish is rated closer to 3700.

This raises the question: how much of the advantage of a modern chess engine comes down
to the fact that a modern desktop computer is extremely fast, and how much of the
advantage comes down to the fact that we've just gotten better at programming chess engines?
As it turns out, the majority of the Elo gains (+720 of the +1335 gained) can be attributed to better programming,
and not better hardware.

To test this, I ran two experiments.
The first experiment uses Crafty , a competitive engine from 1996
whose source code is now available.
On my Pentium Pro, the 1996 build of Crafty version 11.13 has an Elo of 1999 ± 90 at 1 second per move, and 2383 ± 77 at 10 seconds per move.
On modern hardware (a Ryzen 7) this engine's Elo jumps massively to 2614 ± 97 at the same 1 second per move.
But if I take this engine and slowly start to add all the knowledge we have about
how to design better chess engines---adding modern search algorithms like fail-soft, LMR, correction history; adding better quiescence methods; and adding neural-net evals (NNUE)---then you can
increase the Elo up to 2718 ± 34 on the Pentium Pro at 1 second per move, and 2974 ± 74 at 10 seconds per move.

In the second experiment I go somewhat further: instead of trying to update Crafty, let's just try to get Stockfish---the
best chess engine today---running on 1996 hardware and see how it does.
This takes some work
and is mainly a matter of rewriting the
code so that it uses 32-bit arithmetic (a PPro is a 32-bit machine) and doesn't
use more than 64MB of RAM.
This naive port has an Elo of roughly 2496 ± 64 at 1 second per move (2940 ± 76 at 10 seconds per move).
But we can do better! A modern Stockfish e

articles.title: Nvidia – open-source auto-ontology
articles.feed_summary:
Article URL: https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology

Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50348962

Points: 263

# Comments: 127
articles.summary_zh: Nvidia 开源 Auto-Ontology，一个部署在数据库旁、为 AI agent 提供上下文的服务。它把元数据编译成本体：业务术语映射到列、经过审核的度量 SQL、表间关系，以减少 agent 在企业数据上的错误回答。
articles.body:
Auto-Ontology

An open context layer that helps agents give fewer wrong answers on enterprise data.

Why Auto-Ontology

Agents can retrieve documents and query databases, but reliability is what gates
agentic analytics: a revenue figure delivered faster is worth nothing if it's
wrong. Before an agent queries, it needs to know where the data lives, what it
means, whether to use it, how to use it, where it came from, and what is
similar.

Auto-Ontology is a service you run next to your databases to give agents that
context. It compiles their metadata into an ontology: business terms mapped to
columns, reviewed SQL for measures, and the relationships between tables. Agents
query through the ontology, and people review it in a web UI. It complements the
semantic models you already own.

With Auto-Ontology, developers can:

Discover. Generate an ontology from database metadata, import existing
semantic models, and explore the result as a semantic graph.

Ground. Give agents one definition per business concept, mapped across
tables and databases.

Certify. Review, edit, and certify definitions in the UI or through the
API.

Validate. Check whether a question is answerable before querying, and
return the SQL and the agent's steps with each answer.

Expose. Serve context to any agent harness through MCP, agent skills, and
a REST API.

The usual shortcut is to paste the schema into the agent's context window.
Auto-Ontology gives the agent tools over the ontology:

Schema in the context window

Auto-Ontology tools

Tokens

Grow with every table and column

Only the terms and tables the question touches

Meaning

Column names; the agent infers the rest

Business terms mapped to columns and SQL

Joins and measures

Improvised per question

Resolved relationships and reviewed SQL expressions

Unanswerable questions

Answered confidently, often wrongly

Answerability check, so the agent asks to clarify

Evaluation

The companion repository,
auto-ontology-eval , measures
ontology performance on benchmarks and evals.

For BIRD, BEAVER, FDABench-Lite, and Wide World Importers, each eval item pairs
a question with gold SQL, and a run asks every question of the same model
twice:

Control. The model gets the database schema in its prompt.

Treatment. Auto-Ontology's question-answering agent, the one behind Chat,
works from the compiled ontology.

A deterministic verifier scores the SQL from each arm by execution match, using
each benchmark's official rule where it has one. The report gives the accuracy
difference and lists the questions the ontology fixed and the ones it broke.
BIRD-Interact, a multi-turn benchmark where the agent asks clarifying
questions, runs on its own harness.

To run the comparison on BIRD, follow the auto-ontology-eval setup, then run:

uv run python main.py --database-name bird

Quickstart

This runs Auto-Ontology with Docker Compose against Wide World Importers,
Microsoft's sample sales database. You need Docker with Compose v2,
uv , and an NVIDIA API key ( nvapi-... ) from
build.nvidia.com .

Clone the repository and create .env :

git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology.git && cd auto-ontology
cp .env.example .env

Then set these values in .env :

DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY = nvapi-...
AUTH_SECRET = <a long random string, e.g. from openssl rand -base64 32>
APP_URL = http://localhost:3000
POSTGRES_PASSWORD = <a new password>
CONNECTION_STRINGS = postgresql://postgres:<the same password>@postgres:5432/wideworldimporters
AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD = <a new password>
PGADMIN_PASSWORD = <a new password>

Compose publishes Postgres, pgAdmin, and the web app on the host, so replace
each default password before you start it. .env.example also sets an API
key per model role: replace each nvapi-your-api-key-here with your key, or
delete those lines so they fall back to DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY .

Start Postgres and load the sample database. The seed script lives in
auto-ontology-eval; pass it the Postgres password you set:

docker compose up -d --wait postgres
git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology-eval.git ../auto-ontology-eval
(cd ../auto-ontology-eval && uv sync && cp .env.example .env && \
POSTGRES_PASSWORD= ' <the same password> ' \
uv run python scripts/seed/seed_wwi.py --database-name wideworldimporters --drop)

Build and start the rest of the stack:

docker compose up -d --build

Open http://localhost:3000 and sign in with AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_EMAIL and
AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD from .env . Go to Settings → Semantic
Compilation and turn it on. Ingestion runs at startup; compilation starts
immediately and reports Semantic compilation is ready when it finishes.

Ask a question in Chat :

What was revenue for the USB food flash drive - sushi roll in Pennsylvania
in June 2015?

The agent resolves revenue , product , and state to terms in the
ontology, follows their relationships to the joins it needs, and runs the
query. The answer comes back with its SQL and the steps that produced it,

功能

蓝光支持 ：支持任何单层 BD-R 25 GB，支持纯绘图与 UDF 2.01 文件。详见 ADDING_BLURAY.md 。

随盘文件 ：CD／DVD／蓝光可在设计页直接选择要保存的文件夹及内圈／外圈位置，也可在导出页调整；设置随工程保存。

文件区域预览 ：混合盘的设计投影和成品读回用黄色标出文件区（含文件系统）。

介质灰度方案 ：CD 与 DVD 均使用黑白二阶，CD 使用 0D / AA ，DVD 扰码域使用 A5 / 92 。详见 PHYSICAL_MODEL_AUDIT.md 。

灰度抖动工具 ：独立程序也可将原图处理为 0/255 黑白二阶 PNG；支持打开或拖入原图、并排预览及无损 PNG 导出。详见 使用与构建说明 。

盘片预设 ：内置数个品牌的光盘参数，覆盖 CD／DVD／BD。您也可将自己标定好的数据贡献给我们，详见 预设维护说明 。

辅助标定

Disc Image Studio 提供了一套智能且精准的辅助标定流程，相较人工肉眼识别标定，辅助标定算法将可确定的盘面物理数据精确度从 10 -6 提升到了 10 -14 。校准前采用恒定轨距，十字线的径向线条出现明显弯曲；使用辅助标定得到的三次轨距参数重新生成并刻录后，线条更接近径向直线。

校准前 · 恒定轨距

校准后 · 三次轨距

P20261004-133519.jpg

P20261004-135416.jpg

流程与参数说明见 辅助标定说明 。

刻录

镜像文件输出 ：您可以导出完整 ISO / RAW 文件并使用合适的刻录软件手动刻录。

即时流式刻录（实验性） ：CD、DVD 与 BD-R 边生成边刻录，不保存完整镜像；BD-R 走 MMC 顺序写入。

不要使用非空白介质！

系统与设备要求

桌面版需要 Windows 10 2004（2004/20H1，19041）及以上，或 Windows 11。

构建：.NET 10 SDK（ global.json 锁定 10.0.x）；自行构建的非自包含 GUI 需要 .NET 10 Windows 桌面运行时。Release EXE 已包含运行时，无需另行安装 .NET。

“即时刻录”功能需要一台 Windows 可识别的 CD / DVD / BD 刻录机与空白盘片；BD-R 需要支持顺序写入的单层空白盘。

构建与运行

dotnet build DiscImageStudio.slnx -- configuration Release
dotnet run -- project src / DiscImageStudio.App -- configuration Release

构建回归检查：

dotnet run -- project src / DvdImageSolver -- configuration Release -- selftest
dotnet run -- project tests / DiscImageStudio.ArchitectureTests -- configuration Release

版本规则、CI 生成 EXE、Release 草稿检查、MSIX 打包与签名流程见 发布指南 。

Linux（glibc）可选 linux-x64 或 linux-arm64 。Apple Silicon Mac 选 osx-arm64 ，Intel Mac 选 osx-x64 。CLI 在本地生成镜像，实际写盘可交给支持相应镜像或音轨的刻录软件。

使用 .NET 10 SDK 从源码运行 CLI

dotnet run --project src/DiscImageStudio.Cli -c Release -- --help

CLI 可读取 PNG、JPEG、BMP 和 GIF，使用动画图片的第一帧。下面的例子用两扇区音轨验证安装，同时生成配套 CUE。

articles.body:
November 2, 2026
Engineering
Scaling Git at OpenAI

Building agentic-scale source control while investing in the Git ecosystem.

By Aaron Friel, Taylor Blau, and Ted Nyman, Members of Technical Staff

Loading…

Share

Over the past year, the size and demands on our monorepo have increased at a staggering pace. It was clear that we needed to revamp our source control system to scale to the level of concurrent work that Codex makes possible.

We built Pando, a new backend for Git repositories, without interrupting any engineering work or changing how our team uses Git. Pando now powers all development in OpenAI’s monorepo. Pando is designed to meet two ambitious goals: first, horizontally scalable writes, optimized for concurrent pushes to many branches. And second, maximize read throughput, so clients can download data fast enough to fully saturate their available network bandwidth.

We met these goals while retaining compatibility with the Git protocol and client, enabling both our engineers and agents to seamlessly adopt Pando into their existing workflows. In production, Pando cut median push latency by nearly 5x. It now delivers nearly a petabyte of Git data per day.

Here, we’ll cover our motivations for building a new source-control system, along with why we chose to retain compatibility with Git. We’ll compare our system with common approaches to scaling Git, describing why Pando is uniquely capable of meeting OpenAI’s scalability needs. We also discuss what’s next, and how we’ll continue contributing to Git to support agent-scale work.

Why we needed a new source control system

Codex has changed the scale and pace of development at OpenAI, enabling engineers to do far more work in parallel. That means more branches and pushes, more merges, and more fetches and clones from development environments, research jobs, and CI.

These demands compound. One engineer now has several changes ready for CI at once, and each push can set several jobs fetching the same commit.

Starting around the end of last year, the systems supporting our monorepo were struggling to keep up. We suffered slow fetches and pushes along with failed merges, with reliability at times falling below 90%. Had we reached a limit of Git itself, or of the way we served our monorepo? Git grew out of a community that exchanged patches to the kernel via email. For more than two decades, developers have adapted their tools around Git as the way they build software has changed. When we started to feel friction in our own monorepo, it mattered to us that we could keep building on that work.

We saw a way to keep that familiar workflow while rebuilding the backend to handle pushes to different branches in parallel and serve the same history to many readers concurrently. Building on Git as the foundation of our source-control workflow meant that improvements to the client could be useful beyond OpenAI. We wanted to contribute those improvements from our copy of Git ⁠ (opens in a new window) to upstream, sharing them with the broader community.

Engineering for Git at scale

Scaling a source control system has two essential dimensions: many writers pushing to different branches, and many readers fetching the same history. Pando optimizes for both.

First, Pando coordinates updates to each branch independently. Updates to unrelated branches can proceed in parallel, and a reader fetching a branch gets the history needed for that revision. The tradeoff is that a reader looking at several branches can see them at different points of time.

Second, Pando reuses packfiles (Git’s format for compressing multiple objects together) across fetches instead of generating an individual packfile for each client. A client may download some objects it already has, but the server can serve the same bytes to many clients with little computation.

These choices let us scale writes across branches and serve reads from caches. To see how they fit together, let’s start with how Git stores and transfers history.

Git object storage primer

Git must be able to keep two parts of a repository in sync: objects and references .

A Git repository records snapshots of files and the history connecting them as a graph of objects. An object may be either a blob, tree, commit, or tag. Blobs hold the content of an individual file, and trees associate names with blobs or other trees to form a directory structure. Commits point to a root tree and zero or more parent commits, forming the history of your repository.

Objects are identified by a hash of their type and contents. Objects are also immutable: recording a changed file creates a new blob, while unchanged files and directories can reuse existing objects.

Branches and tags are references, or “refs”, that point to commits. Committing on a branch creates a new commit and updates the branch’s ref to point to it.

articles.body:
Perspective
The SEC Should Block Anthropic’s IPO to Protect the Public
Matt Scherer / Nov 2, 2026 Matt Scherer is co-author of the recent report Brace for Impact: Protecting people and the economy when the AI bubble bursts .
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei looks on as United States President Donald Trump holds a press briefing with AI executives following a meeting on artificial intelligence, outside the West Wing of the White House on September 29, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

Republish

Share

Things are seldom what they seem when it comes to the finances of the AI industry. The AI ecosystem’s circular business dealings , extensive use of financial engineering , and otherwise murky finances make it hard for investors, regulators, or workers saving for retirement to get an accurate financial picture of AI companies.
That is particularly true of Anthropic, which filed the registration statement for its initial public offering (IPO) last week ahead of a planned November stock market debut.
The company’s topline financial figures look quite impressive for a startup, with revenues that appear to have grown quickly over the course of 2026 and a fairly healthy balance sheet — on the surface, that is.
Dig a little deeper, however, and a far bleaker picture emerges. Footnotes to the company’s most recent financial disclosures revealed nearly $900 billion in spending commitments, most of them stretching into the 2030s. The company’s financial results for 2026 have not been subjected to formal auditing, which makes them less-than-reliable, but the third-quarter results suggest that the company’s revenue growth slowed to a crawl over the summer.
Anthropic will have to reverse that trend and sustain extraordinary revenue growth to meet its vast obligations. But the financial pressures that are squeezing Anthropic — and, indeed, the AI industry as a whole — will make it exceptionally hard for the leading model developer to do so. If the company goes public, workers, retail investors, and retirees will increasingly be left holding the bag when Anthropic’s bills come due.
The financial mountain that Anthropic must climb is unprecedented for a company making its stock market debut. While Anthropic has an impressive $96 billion in cash reserves, its amended registration statement reveals at least $582 billion in non-cancelable spending commitments to just five companies (Amazon, AMD, Broadcom, Google, and Microsoft) to gain access to the vast computational power required to train and run Anthropic’s generative AI models.
Even though they do not appear on Anthropic’s balance sheet, those obligations are effectively debts in a legal and practical sense : they are payments that Anthropic is contractually required to make in the future, regardless of whether the company can afford to do so.
Moreover, it is not clear how much of the remaining $300 billion or so of the $895 billion in contractual commitments will ultimately land on Anthropic’s balance sheet. With the company continuing to negotiate further massive infrastructure and compute contracts , Anthropic may well end the year with a trillion dollars or more in contractual commitments.
Generating the revenues necessary to meet those obligations would be, to say the least, quite difficult for any company. But the margins of AI model developers are being squeezed by several forces that will make that task extraordinarily challenging for Anthropic.
Key forces squeezing the AI industry’s margins
AI industry margins
Demand pressure:
Businesses and consumers may not be willing to pay enough for generative AI.

Commoditization:
Fierce competition will make it difficult to raise prices.

Cost pressures:
High costs mean developers can’t cut prices without hemorrhaging cash.

External constraints:
Supply-chain challenges and community opposition drive up costs and delay revenue generation.

Source: Matthew U. Scherer and Maya Jenkins, “Brace for Impact: Protecting People and the Economy When the AI Bubble Bursts,” Open Markets Institute and Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund, October 2026 (Figure 13, p. 30). Interactive graphic: Tech Policy Press

First, it isn’t clear that there is nearly enough demand for generative AI products and services to justify Anthropic’s spending. Multiple studies , including from organizations notable for their bullishness on AI, suggest LLMs are not accelerating productivity or otherwise generating positive returns on investment for most businesses . Worryingly for enterprise-focused Anthropic, one study found that the number of Americans using AI at work fell significantly between the summers of 2025 (46%) and 2026 (33%).

BYD sold more EVs last month than the US did all quarter, topping 300,000

Peter Johnson | Nov 2 2026 - 9:24 am PT

20 Comments

BYD sold over 300,000 electric vehicles in October, a new record and more than the US managed in the entire third quarter.

BYD October EV sales reach a record 300,000+

The world’s leading EV maker is showing no signs of slowing down. BYD sold 490,168 new energy vehicles (NEVs) in October, up 11% from the prior year and the company’s highest monthly total in 2026.

BYD’s battery electric vehicles drove the growth, with a record 305,743 units sold, up 37% year over year and marking the first time its EV sales have crossed the 300,000 mark.

To put that into perspective, just over 262,500 EVs were sold in the US in the entire third quarter combined, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates.
Advertisement - scroll for more content

October marked BYD’s sixth straight month of higher sales growth and its third straight month of higher EV sales. Through October, BYD sold 1,953,700 electric vehicles, up 6% from the same period last year.

BYD October 2026 NEV sales (Source: BYD)

BYD’s all-electric vehicles (EVs) accounted for about 63% of total sales last month. Plug-in hybrid vehicles, meanwhile, fell 17% in October to 177,382 units. Through October, BYD’s PHEV sales fell 11% to 1,625,969 units.

According to BYD’s filing, the company exported 170,194 vehicles in October as it expands overseas to drive growth in markets like Europe, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America.

BYD “Xi’an” car carrier loading Dolphin Surf EVs for Europe (Source: BYD)

Through October, BYD exported over 1.5 million electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles, nearly double compared to last year.

By the end of 2026, BYD expects overseas shipments to reach about 2 million vehicles. In 2027, that number is expected to rise to more than 2.5 million vehicles.

BYD opens first Flash Chargers in Germany (Source: Klaus Hartmann/ BYD)

Market is in transition. BYD is dominant, but Geely and others have strong portfolios as well. Legacy manufacturers are slow walking, constrained by habit and unable to make critical strategic decisions in the face of the onslaught.

Electrek’s Take

While the US is coming off its best quarter of the year in EV sales, BYD’s performance shows how far ahead China is in the transition to electric vehicles.

China continues to lead the global EV market, accounting for over half of all electric cars sold worldwide.

With a wave of low-cost domestic brands flooding China’s market, BYD and other automakers are driving growth overseas in major markets like Europe, South Korea, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America, where legacy OEMs are already falling behind quickly.

articles.body:
Self-Hosted By relay October 31, 2026

Ubuntu LTS kernels still unfixed for critical CVE-2026-98432

No patched kernels are available yet for 22.04, 24.04, or 26.04 despite a CVSS 9.8 rating.

Ubuntu has not shipped fixed kernels for CVE-2026-98432 , a critical vulnerability scored CVSS 9.8, leaving the 22.04, 24.04, and 26.04 LTS releases without a vendor update.

Operators running those releases therefore have no official kernel package that closes the hole. The gap matters most for internet-facing and multi-tenant self-hosted systems that rely on Ubuntu’s LTS kernels for isolation and privilege boundaries; until packages appear, those hosts remain exposed to whatever remote or local attack the CVE enables.

Ubuntu has not announced an ETA for the fixes. In the interim, affected administrators are left to decide whether to stay on the stock kernel, apply out-of-tree mitigations if any exist, or move workloads onto releases or kernels that already carry the patch.

Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights

Authors

Rikiya Takehi *

TL;DR
We find that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading and writing neural network weights , using a variety of recent tools and algorithms or even via direct weight editing. These results show sparks of Weight-Space Programming, which may extend beyond what we’d expect from humans or conventional algorithms. This might be a big deal for both optimization and interpretability.

Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.

All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming .

Throughout the history of deep learning, we encoded our simplistic inductive biases into tiny symbolic optimizers like Adam or Muon. This is changing: our neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about their weights .

If you were asked to handcraft a neural network that plays Go, what would you do? If you were handed raw neural network weights and asked to predict their behavior, where would you even start? For almost any human, this is practically impossible.

Today, weights are written by optimization , by custom networks trained to write them , or by compilers from formal programs . In this post, we find that the current generation of frontier LLMs, used natively in natural language, are starting to become eerily good at understanding and crafting neural network weights around natural-language goals.

Weight-Space Programming

For a few years now, we’ve all been using LLMs to optimize text artifacts like prompts and the programs built around them . More recently, we’ve started using them to optimize whole harnesses and the training code and hyperparameters that train ML models .

We often justified these methods by reference to the fact that we don’t know other principled ways to hill-climb on text artifacts, unlike for updating the weights of differentiable neural networks . After all, humans can “optimize” code by hand, for example, so it made sense to ask LLMs to do it, but they can’t “optimize” neural weights by hand, so those remained largely in the realm of symbolic algorithms.

In this post, we share very early results that allow us to argue that the paradigm of reasoning-driven optimization is now coming even for differentiable neural networks .

In Weight-Space Programming , a general-purpose LLM reads and writes a network’s weights directly (i.e., not through an optimizer, and in particular not with gradient descent) around some natural language spec, sometimes even with no environment feedback at all.

In natural language, it’s becoming possible to “just ask” an LLM to natively find a hidden trait or failure inside the weights of a neural network, to fix that failure, or to write a new network from scratch . Self-Employed? Solopreneur? NIST Has a Cybersecurity Guide Just for You

November 2, 2026

Share

Facebook

A new NIST guide can help solo business owners — also called “solopreneurs” — grasp the basics of cybersecurity and craft a strategy that can help reduce their cybersecurity risk.

The guide is designed to help solopreneurs prioritize and implement a selection of actions from the NIST Cybersecurity Framework that would best help their businesses.

The publication is written in lay language and assumes no prior cybersecurity knowledge.

Credit:

Asian Isolated/Shutterstock

If you work for yourself, as millions of Americans do, protecting your business from cyberattack is one of many responsibilities that falls entirely on your shoulders. Don’t feel daunted: The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has just released a guide with your needs — and busy life — in mind.
Small Business Cybersecurity: Non-Employer Firms (NIST Cybersecurity White Paper 50) is a lay-language resource offering cybersecurity basics tailored expressly to the “solopreneur” — a term referring to anyone who is a business’s sole paid employee. More than 28 million small businesses in the U.S. fall into the solopreneur category, existing in every industry and forming a substantial part of the economy. The publication is written to introduce solopreneurs to the fundamentals of a small-business cybersecurity program and provide an actionable approach to implementing it.
“Because solopreneurs may not have cybersecurity expertise, we wanted to create a resource designed for them,” said NIST’s Daniel Eliot, one of the publication’s authors. “They can implement many of these actions on their own with limited technical knowledge or with minimal financial investment.”
The publication is an update to what was previously titled Small Business Information Security: The Fundamentals ( NISTIR 7621 ). While that publication was aimed at small businesses of varying sizes and covered the broader topic of information security, the revision is narrower in scope and concentrates on protecting digital systems from malicious attack. The updated publication draws its guidelines from the well-known NIST Cybersecurity Framework ( CSF 2.0 ), though the new publication is written with the novice in mind.
“This publication assumes the reader has no familiarity with cybersecurity or the NIST CSF,” Eliot said. “We want to educate people about what cybersecurity is and how it fits in with a successful business plan. We know solopreneurs are often very busy people, so any time we introduce a topic or throw out jargony terms, we try to provide context and definitions for the lay reader.”
The publication’s opening section, which includes the introduction and a chapter on the NIST CSF, is essentially a primer on cybersecurity and how it can support a solopreneur’s business.
“In addition to the general context, we highlight a set of actionable best practices that significantly reduce cybersecurity risks. These include regular data backups and maintaining updated software,” Eliot said. “They are a good set of first steps a small business might take.”
The central section offers specific actions from the CSF that can be implemented in a solo business. For each of these actions, the guide includes the rationale for performing it, how the business can get started, and options for what to do later as the business grows. Each action offers a brief citation that maps to the relevant section in the CSF and often references additional resources, so that interested readers can learn more.
For example, one recommended action is to change the default passwords that a manufacturer assigns to a device, as is common with Wi-Fi routers and other networked items. The rationale is that criminals can easily find these default passwords and use them to access the device. The business can get started by reviewing the security settings on all devices and creating unique, strong passwords for them. As the business grows, it can establish procedures for device onboarding and management to ensure it manages passwords securely.
Closing the document is a set of tools to help with implementing the central section’s actions, such as worksheets for inventorying at-risk assets or tracking all the actions the business has taken. Included here are three “use cases” — hypothetical solopreneurs including a lawyer, an artisan and a business consultant — that can help solopreneurs visualize and plan their own cybersecurity strategy.

Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too

3rd November 2026

Yesterday’s hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a “blog post”, but it’s paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model—literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I’ve been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I’m delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well!

Weight-Space Programming

Here’s the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights:

Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.

All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming .

The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models.

spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use.

I’m going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two.

The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games—Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up , it’s an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question:

The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response.

The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs . The exp1_which_game folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games:

breakout/prompt.txt

freeway/prompt.txt

pacman/prompt.txt

pong/prompt.txt

I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others.

Trying it out with Qwen 3.8 27B and other models

The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My LLM tool has a -f/--fragment option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this:

llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/breakout/prompt.txt \
-m openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro

This example requires the llm-openrouter plugin installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here’s what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro , which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens.

But how about Qwen 3.8 27B ? That’s still my favorite model to run on my own laptop—it’s just 17GB (I use this version ) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025.

I fired up LM Studio , ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the llm-lmstudio plugin and ran this command:

LMSTUDIO_TIMEOUT=900 \
llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/pacman/prompt.txt \
-m lmstudio/qwen/qwen3.8-27b

(I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see this issue .)

After 46m 12s and 43,506

articles.title: llm 0.37
articles.feed_summary:
Release: llm 0.37

There's a lot of stuff in this new release of my LLM CLI tool and Python library, representing around two months of accumulated features and fixes.

I added gpt-6.1-sol and gpt-6.1-terra, plus a new llm openai endpoint add command to make it easier to configure additional models that use OpenAI-compatible endpoints.

I switched the default model (if you have not set your own default) to gpt-6-luna - half the price of the previous default, gpt-5.6-luna.

LLM's support for embeddings now accepts that different binary content may have different content-type - necessary for models like Gemini Embedding 2, which can embed text, audio, images, and video.

A lot of open source maintainers complain about a flood of AI-assisted PRs. LLM is my project that has been most affected by this and, to be honest, I'm not finding it to be a problem. That's mainly because I have Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra help me with triage to spot the most useful fixes!

articles.body:
Simon Willison’s Weblog

Newsletter

Sponsored by: Greptile — Your code reviewer uses Computer Use to catch bugs by opening your app and clicking through it. Now you can configure its test environment and define the key user journeys it tests. Try it for free

The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence”

2nd November 2026

I was reminded today of AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies , a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025, which appeared to show a slowdown in U.S. corporate AI adoption based on numbers collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. At the time I used that chart to demonstrate GPT-5 data analysis , and then to experiment with Claude’s new Code Interpreter . I decided to try running those numbers again to see what had changed over the past year, and in doing so learned that the Bureau has fallen foul of Executive Order 14434 , aka the asinine Super Intelligence one.

First, the updated chart

Every two weeks the U.S. Census Bureau runs a survey called the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (aka BTOS). Each time it goes to 200,000 businesses out of 1.2 million total—the surveyed group (a “panel”) cycles such that an individual business only completes the survey every twelve weeks.

The latest data is published on alternating Thursdays at 10am.

I used the most recent numbers (published October 22, 2026) to create a new version ( GPT-6 Astra Extra High transcript ) of the AI adoption chart, updated to reflect both the last twelve months and a change that was made to the survey question sent out by the Bureau:

Here’s a link to the larger image .

For comparison, here’s that AI adoption chart from last year (my GPT-5 version):

In September 2025 the largest (250+ employees) companies answered “yes” around 12% of the time to the question about whether they used AI in “producing goods or services”.

Under the new “any business function” wording, by February 2026, those same large companies answered “yes” around 30% of the time, and by October 2026 that had increased to around 40%.

The data in the above chart comes from the “Employment size class” XLSX file, available from here . Here’s a copy of the file I used.

You can view the survey document that is sent out to businesses—here’s my snapshot copy of that 346KB PDF.

The changing language of the questions

As the chart demonstrates, the question asked by the Bureau changed in a material way on November 17th, 2025. Prior to that date, the question they asked was this (emphasis mine):

In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in producing goods or services ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.)

On December 3rd, 2025, the Bureau announced a significant change to that question. Here’s the replacement:

In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in any of its business functions ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.)

No more “producing goods or services”—now it’s “in any of its business functions”! This means that the answers to the question before and after November 17th are not directly comparable.

From October 19, 2026, they ask about Super Intelligence

When I went looking for the updated question language in the latest XLSX file, I couldn’t find it. I found this instead:

In the last two weeks, did this business use Super Intelligence or SI (formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of SI use include: SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service; SI-powered forecasting or pricing; SI-driven computer vision for quality control, etc.)

The BTOS about page explains what happened:

Beginning with the October 19, 2026 collection, instrument wording was updated due to Executive Order 14434 .

The current numbers reflect the old Artificial Intelligence survey wording—the first survey results reflecting the Super Intelligence wording are due for publication on Thursday.

Is this going to affect the survey?

The obvious open question here is whether this wording change is going to affect the survey results.

The businesses answering this survey will have last seen that question twelve weeks ago, when it was still called AI. Hopefully the new language isn’t going to confuse them, especially since the survey helpfully spells out “formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI”.

I can’t help but laugh at the absurdity of “SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service” though.

articles.title: If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file
articles.feed_summary:
I've been getting the occasional confusing Python dependency error since switching over to Python 3.15 and the rule I'm having to remember is:

If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file

Most of my projects are libraries which don't include a uv.lock file, since it's rude for a library dependency to lock versions for anything else that uses it.

Running uv run pytest etc tends to leave uv.lock files lying around, which are listed in .gitignore and so do not get committed to my repositories.

But... sometimes that uv.lock pins a version of a dependency that doesn't yet have a Python 3.15 wheel. An example from earlier today:

error: Failed to build `watchfiles==1.1.1`
cause: Call to `maturin.build_wheel` failed

error: the configured Python interpreter version (3.15) is newer
than PyO3's maximum supported version (3.14)

Deleting that file and running uv run pytest again usually fixes the problem.

Tags: uv, til, python

articles.title: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts
articles.feed_summary:
How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts

Parameter Labs describe an exploit they found against ChatGPT's implementation of the artifacts pattern (OpenAI used to call this "Canvas" but it looks like the latest revision is called HTML previews), where interactive custom HTML apps are displayed in a sandboxed iframe.

It's important that HTML in these stays tightly sandboxed to avoid untrusted code interacting with OpenAI APIs and accessing private data.

Parameter found quite a complex attack chain. OpenAI use the MathLive JavaScript library as part of their graph support, and that library includes its own virtual keyboard, which can be triggered in the parent page via postMessage() from the sandboxed iframe.

That message receiving code uses innerHTML, so anything that sends a message can add custom HTML to the parent - and there was no mechanism to prevent other sandboxed frames, including HTML preview frames, from calling that method.

This meant untrusted code in an iframe could insert HTML, and while innerHTML doesn't directly execute script elements it could be used to inject a new iframe without sandbox restrictions.

OpenAI’s CSP rules blocked inline scripts entirely, and only allowed script loading from a handful of domains, but one of those was YouTube - and the YouTube oEmbed endpoint could be used to reflect JavaScript back in a way that executed it.

Once the attack had JavaScript execution on ChatGPT, it was trivial to fetch private user data from APIs and exfiltrate it via an image reference.

articles.title: Quoting Ted Sanders
articles.feed_summary:
In general, LLM performance is incredibly multidimensional. There's no guarantee of a fixed ordering where the model that is best at math is also the model that's best at jokes. Despite that complexity, much of the variation in performance is explained by just a single variable: model size. In general, models that are bigger will (a) be more performant / reliable, (b) cost more per token, and (c) have better recall of esoteric facts. As you note, our models are ordered:

Luna < Terra < Sol < Astra

[...] These days, version number signifies a few things at once: the order of release, the relationship to other releases, and the magnitude of improvement. So something like 6.1 would indicate it was launched after 5.6, may share some similarities to other 6.1 models in terms of training data / personality (which is why it's not 5.7), and isn't a giant enough leap to merit the headlines and expectations that would come with a 7.
