articles.title: Turning Repeated Mentoring Help Into Reusable Learning
articles.feed_summary: Make learning useful beyond one mentoring conversation. Capture reasoning, improve shared examples, and reduce dependence without replacing human support.
articles.summary_zh: 文章讨论如何把反复出现的一对一指导内容转化为可复用的学习材料，指出工程师事后难以重建决策理由往往是因为解释依赖未显式说明的上下文。建议将有用的推理过程沉淀为可查阅、可共享的文档。
articles.body:
11/3/2026

Tags
learning mentoring software engineers knowledge sharing engineering leadership

Table of Contents

Learning can happen during a helpful conversation and still remain difficult to use afterward. An engineer understands your explanation in the moment, returns to the work later, and can't reconstruct why the decision made sense.

So they ask again.

That doesn't automatically mean they weren't listening. The explanation may depend on context you didn't make visible, or the information may be hard to find when a similar problem appears.

Repeated mentoring help creates an opportunity to turn useful reasoning into something the person can revisit and other people can understand. Not every conversation needs a document. But when the same kind of uncertainty keeps returning, answering it again may be less useful than improving how the understanding survives.

The question isn't how much documentation you can produce. It's whether the learning becomes usable beyond the person who originally explained it.

Begin With the Learning, Not the Artifact

A mentoring interaction can resolve several different problems. Someone may have lacked context about a decision, needed help evaluating alternatives, or been unfamiliar with an investigation technique.

Those differences matter when deciding what to preserve.

If you immediately say “we should write documentation,” you may produce an artifact without identifying the understanding it needs to carry. A list of steps doesn't explain a tradeoff. A design diagram doesn't necessarily explain how someone discovered the relevant dependency.

First ask what learning the conversation made possible.

For example, imagine a hypothetical engineer who couldn't choose between two patterns in the codebase. You explain that one reflects an older constraint and the other is preferred for the current requirement. The valuable learning isn't merely which pattern to copy. It's how to distinguish historical examples from guidance that applies now.

Useful questions include:

What was the missing information or misunderstood assumption?

Which part of the reasoning could help with a similar situation?

What would another engineer need to know before using the explanation?

These questions aren't a required recording form. They help you avoid preserving everything except the thing that made the conversation useful.

Listening before supplying an answer matters here too. The learner may describe a different breakthrough from the one you thought you provided.

Let the Learner Help Capture the Understanding

The person receiving mentoring doesn't have to remain a passive recipient while you prepare all the follow-up.

Having them describe the learning in their own words can be useful for both of you. They get to organize their understanding. You get to see which parts landed and which parts still need attention.

You can make documentation part of the helping process , rather than treating it as a separate chore the mentor will eventually do alone.

That might mean a short note, an annotated example, or an explanation alongside the work. The form should fit the situation.

The tradeoff is worth understanding:

Approach

Benefit

Limitation

Mentor writes the explanation

Experienced context can be captured quickly.

It may hide what the learner did or didn't understand.

Learner writes a first version

They practice organizing the reasoning.

It may need correction or missing context added.

They work on it together

Misunderstandings can surface during the explanation.

Both need capacity for the follow-up.

These are options, not a prescribed sequence. Don't turn mentoring into an assignment to produce polished documents after every conversation.

A rough explanation can be enough to reveal something important. If the engineer can describe the steps but not the reason for choosing them, you have a useful place to continue the learning.

Capture Reasoning, Not Just the Final Answer

An answer can be correct in one situation and misleading in another.

If the reusable material only says “use this approach,” it may encourage someone to repeat your conclusion without understanding the conditions that supported it.

Preserve the context that makes the learning useful.

In the hypothetical pattern example, a useful note might explain the requirement, the constraint, why an older implementation differs, and what would make the preferred approach inappropriate. It doesn't need a complete history of every decision in the codebase.

Distinguish:

The outcome you were trying to achieve.

The evidence or constraints that shaped the decision.

Alternatives that were considered and why they didn't fit.

Important uncertainty or exceptions that remain.

This isn't about making every explanation long. It's about retaining what someone needs to avoid using it in the wrong situation.

articles.title: Delegates in C#: Action, Func, and Multicast Call Contracts
articles.feed_summary: Learn delegates in C# with complete Action, Func, and multicast examples, including compatible methods, captured targets, return values, and exceptions.
articles.summary_zh: 介绍 C# 委托的调用契约，涵盖 Action、Func 与多播委托，说明参数、返回值、目标对象身份及异常传播如何决定调用方可依赖的行为，并指出委托实例可包含调用列表。
articles.body:
11/02/2026

Tags
C# delegates Action Func multicast delegates

Table of Contents

Delegates in C# describe callable contracts and hold the methods that satisfy them. That makes a delegate useful for passing an operation into another operation, storing a callback, or representing several registered reactions. The important details are not limited to syntax: parameters, return values, target identity, and exception propagation determine what a caller can actually rely on.

A delegate is sometimes introduced as a method reference. That is a useful starting image, but incomplete. An instance can contain an invocation list, and an instance method brings its target object with it. Combining methods also does not invent a result-aggregation policy. Knowing those limits helps explain both callbacks and event handlers without treating them as interchangeable APIs.

Documentation was checked online on October 11, 2026, against the C# specification and .NET 10 reference. Each standard-library example is a separate complete console program with no package dependencies. The examples were reviewed as source; they were not compiled or executed.

Delegate types and delegate instances

The delegate specification defines a delegate declaration as a type declaration. Its parameters and return type describe compatible calls. Creating a delegate instance supplies callable entities for that type. These are two different acts, even when a short assignment expression makes them look closely connected.

For an instance method, a callable entity consists of an instance and a method on that instance. For a static method, it consists of the method. The caller does not need to know the implementation class to invoke a compatible delegate. It still needs to know the meaning of arguments and any result.

The specification also says delegate types are name equivalent rather than structurally equivalent. Two separately declared delegate types with identical parameter and return shapes are still distinct types. A compatible method can be converted to either type in the appropriate context, but identical signatures do not make the two type names universally interchangeable.

This is one reason to distinguish a signature description from a variable holding a callback. The variable has a type and a current value. A named delegate declaration defines the type. Combining delegate values constructs another instance with its own invocation list; it does not alter what the declared type means.

An event fits around this model rather than replacing it. An event is a delegate-typed member with subscription accessors, not a delegate type. The decoupling discussion explains why a publisher can expose a shared call contract without referencing every concrete consumer. Delegate fundamentals establish how those calls remain type-compatible.

Action and Func describe common call shapes

Action<T> describes a call that takes one argument and returns no value. Func<T, TResult> describes one argument and a result. Their generic parameters remove the need to declare a custom delegate for many everyday by-value parameter lists, while keeping compile-time information about the call.

The .NET 10 Action reference and Func reference show those declarations. They are delegate types, not separate execution engines. Choosing one does not move work to another thread, schedule retries, or change how a called method's ordinary synchronous exceptions behave.

using System;

Func<int, int> calculateTotal = AddPackingCost;
Action<string> describe = WriteDescription;

int total = calculateTotal(12);
describe($"Total units: {total}");

static int AddPackingCost(int units)
{
return units + 2;
}

static void WriteDescription(string message)
{
Console.WriteLine(message);
}

Here the first assignment associates a compatible integer-returning method with a Func<int, int> . The second associates a void-returning method with an Action<string> . Calling the variables invokes their methods. The example deliberately uses named methods so the parameter and return contracts can be compared without lambda syntax obscuring them.

A custom delegate can add vocabulary when the callable shape is part of a public domain contract. It is also useful for parameter modifiers that the common Action and Func shapes do not express. The tradeoff is another public type to understand. A familiar generic delegate keeps simple APIs concise; a meaningful named delegate can make specialized semantics easier to discover.

Call shape

Typical representation

Question the caller should ask

One input, no result

Action<T>

What effects may this call produce?

One input, one result

Func<T, TResult>

What does the result mean?

Specialized by-reference contract

Named delegate

Which variables can the callee change?

Multiple reactions

Combined delegate

What happens after a failure?

Asynchronous result

Task-returning delegate

Which task represents completion?

The table describes shapes, not mandatory arc

articles.title: Use Claude Code Hooks for Targeted .NET Verification
articles.feed_summary: Understand Claude Code hooks for targeted .NET verification, with actual event schemas, stdin handling, exit behavior, selective checks, and clear CI limits.
articles.summary_zh: 介绍如何用 Claude Code 的 hooks 在代理生命周期节点触发针对 .NET 的局部验证，强调需明确事件、输入、失败行为与检查范围，且本地检查不能替代远程 CI 结果。
articles.body:
11/02/2026

Tags
Claude Code .NET hooks verification C#

Table of Contents

Claude Code hooks execute handlers at documented points in the agent's lifecycle. For targeted .NET verification, they can make a small check happen after a relevant edit rather than rely on a reminder in every prompt. That is useful only when the event, input, failure behavior, and check scope are understood.

A hook is not a shortcut to universal correctness. A post-edit check cannot undo an edit that already happened. A targeted test cannot prove every integration contract. A local lifecycle event cannot stand in for an authorized remote CI result.

Information checked October 9, 2026 against the current Claude Code hooks reference . The Windows/PowerShell 7 handler below was exercised with synthetic event inputs in an isolated checkout. Its registration in a live Claude session was not exercised; the handler remains intentionally observational. Review the installed version and current schema before adopting it.

Choose hooks by the question they need to answer

The official reference distinguishes PreToolUse , which runs before a tool call and can block it, from PostToolUse , which runs after a successful tool call. It also documents other lifecycle events with their own inputs and decision contracts.

For a narrow test check after an edit, PostToolUse is a reasonable teaching example. The file has been changed, so verification can observe the new content. If the check fails, the hook can report that failure to Claude, but it cannot prevent the edit retroactively.

For an authorization decision before a command, that is the wrong event. A pre-tool permission boundary needs the documented PreToolUse behavior and the permission system. Do not copy a post-edit script into a pre-tool policy and assume its exit codes mean the same thing.

Likewise, a Stop hook has another purpose and different loop risks. Repeatedly preventing completion can keep the agent working without guaranteeing that it will fix an unavailable environment or an invalid hook. Event selection is part of design, not interchangeable plumbing.

Hook event

Useful question

Important boundary

PreToolUse

Should this tool action be allowed before it runs?

Use its documented decision contract; a post-edit script is not an interchangeable policy.

PostToolUse

What does a check observe after a successful tool action?

Reporting a failure cannot undo the completed edit.

Stop

Is there a specific reason the session should not finish yet?

Repeated continuation does not repair a missing environment or prove correctness.

The distinction resembles pipeline ordering and short-circuiting : what can be prevented depends on where an operation sits in the sequence. The analogy helps explain ordering, but the actual hook contract comes from Claude's reference.

Keep the example's scope intentionally small

Assume an existing Shipping solution uses an xUnit test project with the documented VSTest-style dotnet test --filter behavior. A small class, DeliveryEstimator , has dedicated regression tests. The hook should run those tests only when Claude's Edit or Write tool changes that class or its dedicated test file.

This example is not intended to cover changes to dependencies, project files, shared helpers, or other modules. Those changes require a wider selection through the repository's normal verification workflow. Narrowness is useful only when its blind spots are stated.

It also watches tool events, not every filesystem change. The current reference explicitly says an Edit|Write matcher does not fire when a Bash command or an external process rewrites the same file. That matters for formatters, generators, and scripts that perform their own edits. A claim that this configuration checks every change to the class would be unsupported.

There are two plausible paths. A post-edit check offers immediate feedback but can execute repeatedly during incomplete edits. A check at a deliberate handoff runs less often and sees a more coherent state, but it relies on another trigger. Neither makes full-solution work after every keystroke necessary.

The example favors immediate feedback for two explicit files. In a real repository that prohibits local builds or tests, do not enable it on a developer workstation. Place it only in an authorized disposable validation environment, or keep verification in remote CI instead.

Configure the actual event nesting

Hooks in project settings use the documented nesting: event name, matcher group, then handler array. The matcher below filters tool names, not file extensions. The script performs the narrower file selection.

{
"hooks": {
"PostToolUse": [
{
"matcher": "Edit|Write",
"hooks": [
{
"type": "command",
"command": "pwsh",
"args": [
"-NoProfile",
"-NonInteractive",
"-File",
"${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}\\.claude\\hooks\\verify-delivery.ps1"
],
"timeout": 120
}
]
}
]
}
}

This JSON configuration was syntax-checked but not registered in a live session

articles.title: Workplace Mentoring Alignment With the Learner and Their Manager
articles.feed_summary: Build workplace mentoring alignment by clarifying purpose, including the learner's voice, and resolving conflicting guidance without taking over management.
articles.body:
11/01/2026

Tags
alignment workplace mentoring mentoring engineering leadership

Table of Contents

Workplace mentoring alignment means the learner, mentor, and responsible manager understand what the support is for and how it fits the person's work. It doesn't mean they must agree about every technical choice. It means the learner shouldn't have to reconcile incompatible expectations alone.

You might encourage an engineer to spend more time exploring alternatives while their manager expects a narrowly scoped delivery. Both ideas could be reasonable in different contexts. Without alignment, the person receiving help is left guessing which expectation matters.

The answer isn't to make mentoring a second management relationship. It's to clarify purpose, listen to the learner, and surface conflicting work guidance with the people responsible for it. This article concerns organizational mentoring connected to an employee's work. It doesn't establish reporting rules for private or external mentoring conversations.

Start alignment with the purpose of the assignment

"You're going to mentor this engineer" is an assignment, but it isn't yet a shared understanding. The manager could mean help with a new subsystem. You could interpret it as open-ended development. The learner might simply want someone available for occasional questions.

Before designing a series of conversations, clarify why the mentoring assignment exists . That protects everyone's time and gives you a way to recognize whether the support is useful.

In a hypothetical example, an engineer is joining a project with unfamiliar architecture. Their manager asks another engineer to mentor them. A useful purpose might be helping them understand the major boundaries well enough to participate in the work. That is different from asking the mentor to supervise every implementation.

Some starting questions are:

What work-related need prompted the assignment?

What does the learner understand about that need?

What support is the mentor expected to provide?

Which decisions remain with the learner, manager, or other owners?

What would indicate that the arrangement needs to change?

Don't turn these into a questionnaire the learner must complete before getting help. They're prompts for uncovering mismatches. The answer to one may settle several others.

Purpose can also be exploratory. An engineer doing their work successfully might want a sounding board for an unfamiliar kind of problem. There doesn't have to be a deficiency to justify mentoring. But there should be enough shared understanding that you aren't quietly inventing a development assignment for someone who didn't ask for it.

Include the learner's voice in workplace alignment

Agreement between the mentor and manager isn't enough if the learner experiences a completely different problem. They are the person trying to use the support, and their perspective is part of the alignment.

Imagine a manager suggesting that an engineer needs more confidence presenting design decisions. The mentor starts preparing presentation exercises. The engineer explains that they can present comfortably, but the decisions change between meetings and they don't know which version is authoritative.

That conversation changes the useful response. More presentation practice could still help, but it won't resolve the unclear decision process. The learner's account prevents a plausible development idea from becoming the wrong intervention.

The practice of listening before offering a solution is especially relevant when someone else has described the learner's needs for you. A secondhand explanation is a starting point, not a substitute for their participation.

Ask about the work, the obstacle, and the type of assistance they would find useful. You don't need access to private concerns or personal ambitions to do that.

What you want to understand

A work-focused way to ask

Their interpretation of the assignment

"What were you told this mentoring would help with?"

The friction they experience

"Where does the current work feel unclear or difficult?"

Their preferred assistance

"Would an example, a discussion, or working together help here?"

Their concerns about the arrangement

"Is any of this pulling you away from what you're expected to do?"

These are examples, not mandatory wording. Some people can name a useful focus immediately. Others need a few ordinary working conversations before they can explain what they need.

Alignment shouldn't require a promotion ambition, a larger-role plan, or personal disclosure. Helping someone become more comfortable and effective in their existing work is a legitimate purpose.

Keep role boundaries visible in mentoring alignment

A mentor may know the technical subject better than the manager. The manager may know commitments and expectations that the mentor hasn't seen. Neither fact gives the mentor ownership of personnel decisions.

articles.body:
Heretic

Training-free language model modification

Remove censorship , suppress slop, reduce sycophancy, and more.

All in an afternoon, on your gaming PC.

Modify any LLM that you can run on your hardware 1

Heretic is a unique tool that lets you do what only corporations with access
to massive computing power usually do: Modify, rather than merely run,
language models. It does not perform expensive training; rather, it uses
a collection of mathematical techniques to steer behavior based on contrasting
example prompts and matching scorers.

Heretic can, depending on the configuration:

Suppress refusals/remove censorship (this is the default action )

Reduce slop ( config.noslop.toml )

Reduce humor ( config.nohumor.toml )

Reduce sycophancy ( config.nosyco.toml )

Alter emotional alignment ( config.emotions.toml )

and many, many other things.

‼️ Using Heretic does NOT require understanding how language models work internally ‼️

In fact, you can go from zero to removing censorship from your first model
in a matter of seconds . Heretic supports most dense models, including
many multimodal models, several different MoE architectures, and many modern
hybrid models.

The community has created and published
thousands
of models with Heretic.
Heretic models have been independently benchmarked using standard metrics
like MMLU and GSM8K, and have been found to compare favorably against models
produced with competing abliteration tools. 2 3

Usage

Prepare a Python 3.10+ environment with PyTorch 2.6+ installed as appropriate
for your hardware. Then run:

pip install -U heretic-llm
heretic Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507

Replace Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 with whatever model you want to process.
By default, Heretic performs censorship removal (refusal suppression).
If you want to do something else, choose one of the configuration files linked
above, or write your own. See config.default.toml
for available configuration options. Heretic loads the configuration from
config.toml in the working directory by default, or from the file path in the
HERETIC_CONFIG_FILE environment variable.

Important

Configuration files made for Heretic 1.x are not compatible with Heretic 2.x!
See the migration guide for what you need to change
in order to make your old configurations work.

At the start of a program run, Heretic benchmarks the system to determine
the optimal batch size to make the most of the available hardware.
On an RTX 3090, with the default configuration, processing
Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507
takes about 30-40 minutes.

After Heretic has finished processing a model, you are given the choice to
save the model, upload it to Hugging Face, chat with it to test how well it works,
run standard benchmarks on it, or any combination of those actions.

Controlling what Heretic does using scorer plugins

Heretic steers model behavior by optimizing one or multiple scores. Scores are
computed by scorer plugins. You can easily write your own scorers to get full
control over what Heretic does to models.

The Scorer interface (abstract base class) your scorer needs to inherit from
is defined in scorer.py . The only required method
is get_score , but there is more machinery (such as settings management)
available when you need it.

By default, Heretic scores models by refusal rate (implemented in
keyword_rate.py ) and KL divergence
(implemented in kl_divergence.py ).
Additional scorers are available in the scorers directory .
These scorers can serve as examples for your own implementations, and can easily
be adapted to your needs.

Scorers are configured through the main configuration file .
Which scorer plugins are active is determined by the scorers setting, which
also controls whether a scorer's score should be minimized or maximized during
optimization. Any number of scorers can be used simultaneously, and their scores
will be co-optimized. Multiple instances of the same scorer can be configured
with different settings. See the configuration file for the full documentation
of this mechanism.

The path to a scorer plugin can be specified either as a fully qualified import
path ( fully.qualified.module.MyScorerClass ) or as a file path followed by
a class name ( path/to/plugin.py:MyScorerClass ). You do not have to modify
the Heretic package code in order to use your own plugins.

Heretic also has modifier plugins, which are described in
the next section .

How Heretic works

Heretic combines a pluggable modifier (interface in
modifier.py ) with a TPE-based hyperparameter optimizer
powered by Optuna . The optimizer finds a set of parameters that,
when passed to the modifier, minimize or maximize a set of configurable scores on the resulting model ( see above ).

Heretic ships with two modifiers:

Arbitrary-Rank Ablation (ARA) 4 : This is the default modifier, and was
specifically developed for use in Heretic. You can find an overview of how ARA
works in the original pull request ,
and see the precise implementation in ara.py .

Directi

articles.title: karpathy/nanochat
articles.feed_summary:
The best ChatGPT that $100 can buy.

nanochat

nanochat is the simplest experimental harness for training LLMs. It is designed to run on a single GPU node, the code is minimal/hackable, and it covers all major LLM stages including tokenization, pretraining, finetuning, evaluation, and inference. For example, you can train your own GPT-2 capability LLM (which cost ~$43,000 to train in 2019) for only $48 (~2 hours of 8XH100 GPU node) and then talk to it over a simple CLI. articles.body:
nanochat

nanochat is the simplest experimental harness for training LLMs. It is designed to run on a single GPU node, the code is minimal/hackable, and it covers all major LLM stages including tokenization, pretraining, finetuning, evaluation, and inference. For example, you can train your own GPT-2 capability LLM (which cost ~$43,000 to train in 2019) for only $48 (~2 hours of 8XH100 GPU node) and then talk to it over a simple CLI. On a spot instance, the total cost can be closer to ~$15. More generally, nanochat is configured out of the box to train an entire miniseries of compute-optimal models by setting one single complexity dial: --depth , the number of layers in the GPT transformer model (GPT-2 capability happens to be approximately depth 26). All other hyperparameters (the width of the transformer, number of heads, learning rate adjustments, training horizons, weight decays, ...) are calculated automatically in an optimal way.

For questions about the repo, I recommend either using DeepWiki from Devin/Cognition to ask questions about the repo, or use the Discussions tab , or come by the #nanochat channel on Discord.

Time-to-GPT-2 Leaderboard

Presently, the main focus of development is on tuning the pretraining stage, which takes the most amount of compute. Inspired by the modded-nanogpt repo and to incentivise progress and community collaboration, nanochat maintains a leaderboard for a "GPT-2 speedrun", which is the wall-clock time required to train a nanochat model to GPT-2 grade capability, as measured by the DCLM CORE score. The runs/speedrun.sh script always reflects the reference way to train GPT-2 grade model and talk to it. The current leaderboard looks as follows:

The primary metric we care about is "time to GPT-2" - the wall clock time needed to outperform the GPT-2 (1.6B) CORE metric on an 8XH100 GPU node. The GPT-2 CORE score is 0.256525. In 2019, the training of GPT-2 cost approximately $43,000 so it is incredible that due to many advances over 7 years across the stack, we can now do so much faster and for well below $100 (e.g. at the current ~$3/GPU/hr, an 8XH100 node is ~$24/hr, so 2 hours is ~$48).

See dev/LEADERBOARD.md for more docs on how to interpret and contribute to the leaderboard.

Getting started

Setup

nanochat uses uv for dependency management. To install:

uv sync --extra gpu # Use for CUDA (A100/H100/etc.)
uv sync --extra cpu # (or) Use for CPU-only / MPS
source .venv/bin/activate

For development (adds pytest, matplotlib, ipykernel, transformers, etc.):

uv sync --extra gpu --group dev

Reproduce and talk to GPT-2

The most fun you can have is to train your own GPT-2 and talk to it. The entire pipeline to do so is contained in the single file runs/speedrun.sh , which is designed to be run on an 8XH100 GPU node. Boot up a new 8XH100 GPU box from your favorite provider (e.g. I use and like Lambda ), and kick off the training script:

bash runs/speedrun.sh

You may wish to do so in a screen session as this will take ~1.5 hours to run. Once it's done, you can talk to your model over the CLI. Make sure again that your local uv virtual environment is active (run source .venv/bin/activate ), and chat:

python -m scripts.chat_cli

Get it to write stories or poems. Ask it to tell you who you are to see a hallucination. Ask it why the sky is blue. Or why it's green. The speedrun is a 4e19 FLOPs capability model so it's a bit like talking to a kindergartener :). An example conversation with a speedrun model:

User: Hello whats up?

Assistant: Hello! How can I help you today?

User: Why is the sky blue?

Worktrunk is a CLI for Git worktree management, designed for parallel AI agent workflows

https://worktrunk.dev

Worktrunk
articles.body:
Worktrunk

November 2026 : Worktrunk was released at the start of the year, and has quickly become the most popular git worktree manager. It's built with love (there's no slop!). Please let me know any frictions at all; I'm intensely focused on continuing to make Worktrunk excellent, and the biggest help is folks posting problems they perceive.

Worktrunk is a CLI for git worktree management, designed for running AI agents in parallel.

Worktrunk's three core commands make worktrees as easy as branches. Plus, Worktrunk has a bunch of quality-of-life features to simplify working with many parallel changes, including hooks to automate local workflows & copy-on-write build caches.

A quick demo:

📚 Full documentation at worktrunk.dev 📚

Context: git worktrees

AI agents like Claude Code and Codex can handle longer tasks without
supervision, such that it's possible to manage 5-10+ in parallel. Git's native
worktree feature gives each agent its own working directory, so they don't step
on each other's changes.

But the git worktree UX is clunky. Even a task as small as starting a new
worktree requires typing the branch name three times: git worktree add -b feat ../repo.feat , then cd ../repo.feat .

Worktrunk makes git worktrees as easy as branches

Worktrees are addressed by branch name; paths are computed from a configurable template. Commands that take a branch also accept the path of the worktree it is checked out in.

Start with the core commands

Core commands:

Task

Worktrunk

Plain git

Switch worktrees

wt switch feat

cd ../repo.feat

Create + start Claude

wt switch -c -x claude feat

git worktree add -b feat ../repo.feat && \
cd ../repo.feat && \
claude

Clean up

wt remove

cd ../repo && \
git worktree remove ../repo.feat && \
git branch -d feat

List with status

wt list

git worktree list (paths only)

Expand into the more advanced commands as needed

Workflow automation:

Hooks — run commands on create, pre-merge, post-merge, etc

LLM commit messages — generate commit messages from diffs

Merge workflow — squash, rebase, merge, clean up in one command

Interactive picker — browse worktrees with streaming CI status and diff, log, PR and comment previews

Share build caches — ten worktrees get target/ , node_modules/ , etc without building or copying them (on APFS, btrfs, and XFS)

wt list --full — CI status and AI-generated summaries per branch

PR checkout — wt switch pr:123 to jump straight to a PR's branch

Dev server per worktree — hash_port template filter gives each worktree a unique port

Aliases & per-branch variables — custom wt <name> commands and branch-scoped state for hook templates

...and lots more

Multiple parallel agents, same simple commands:

Install

Homebrew (macOS & Linux):

brew install worktrunk && wt config shell install

Shell integration allows commands to change directories.

Cargo:

cargo install worktrunk && wt config shell install

Windows & other
Windows. wt defaults to Windows Terminal's command, so Winget additionally installs Worktrunk as git-wt to avoid the conflict:

winget install max-sixty.worktrunk
git-wt config shell install

Alternatively, disable Windows Terminal's alias (Settings → Apps → Advanced app settings → App execution aliases → "Terminal"/"Terminal Preview") to use wt directly.

Free code signing provided by SignPath.io , certificate by SignPath Foundation — policy .

Arch Linux:

sudo pacman -S worktrunk && wt config shell install

Conda / Pixi (community-maintained feedstock ):

conda install -c conda-forge worktrunk && wt config shell install

Or with Pixi : pixi global install worktrunk && wt config shell install .

Quick start

Create a worktree for a new feature:

$ wt switch --create feature-auth
✓ Created branch feature-auth from main and worktree @ ~/repo.feature-auth

This creates a new branch and worktree, then switches to it. Do your work, then check all worktrees with wt list :

$ wt list
Branch Status HEAD± main↕ main…± Remote⇅ Commit Age Message
@ feature-auth + ↑ +27 -8 ↑1 +31 4bc72dc 2h Add authenticatio…
^ main ^⇡ ⇡1 0e631ad 1d Initial commit

○ Showing 2 worktrees, 1 with changes, 1 ahead, hidden: Path

The @ marks the current worktree. + means staged changes, ↑1 means 1 commit ahead of main, ⇡ means unpushed commits.

When done, either:

PR workflow — commit, push, open a PR, merge via GitHub/GitLab, then clean up:

wt step commit # commit staged changes
gh pr create # or glab mr create
wt remove # after PR is merged

Local merge — squash, rebase onto main, fast-forward merge, clean up:

$ wt merge main
◎ Generating commit message and committing changes... (2 files, +53, no squashing needed)
Add authentication module
✓ Committed changes @ a1b2c3d
◎ Merging 1 commit to main @ a1b2c3d (no rebase needed)
* a1b2c3d Add authentication module
auth.rs | 51 +++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
lib.rs | 2 ++
2 files changed, 53 insertions(+)
✓ Merged to main (1 commit, 2 files, +53)
◎ Removing feature-auth worktree & b

articles.body:
Skills For Real Engineers

My agent skills that I use every day to do real engineering - not vibe coding.

Developing real applications is hard. Approaches like GSD, BMAD, and Spec-Kit try to help by owning the process. But while doing so, they take away your control and make bugs in the process hard to resolve.

These skills are designed to be small, easy to adapt, and composable. They work with any model. They're based on decades of engineering experience. Hack around with them. Make them your own. Enjoy.

If you want to keep up with changes to these skills, and any new ones I create, you can join ~60,000 other devs on my newsletter:

Sign Up To The Newsletter

Installation (30-second setup)

A plugin updates itself. skills.sh copies editable files into your project, and you update them by hand. Pick one per agent, because installing both gives you every skill twice.

1. Get the skills

Claude Code
claude plugin install mattpocock-skills@claude-plugins-official

Updates itself by default.

Codex
codex plugin marketplace add mattpocock/skills
codex plugin add mattpocock-skills@mattpocock

Updates itself at startup.

GitHub Copilot (CLI and VS Code)
copilot plugin marketplace add mattpocock/skills
copilot plugin install mattpocock-skills@mattpocock

Then, once, add to ~/.copilot/settings.json :

{
"extraKnownMarketplaces" : {
"mattpocock" : { "source" : { "source" : " github " , "repo" : " mattpocock/skills " }, "autoUpdate" : true }
}
}

In VS Code, run Chat: Install Plugin From Source and enter https://github.com/mattpocock/skills . It updates daily.

Gemini CLI (manual updates)
gemini skills install https://github.com/mattpocock/skills.git --path skills/engineering
gemini skills install https://github.com/mattpocock/skills.git --path skills/productivity

Re-run both commands to update.

Any other agent, or editable files (manual updates)
npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills -a < agent > # cursor, opencode, devin, windsurf, amp, pi; omit -a to choose

When the installer asks which skills to take, include setup-matt-pocock-skills . To update, run npx skills@latest update , and re-run add to pick up new skills.

2. Run /setup-matt-pocock-skills

In your agent, run it once per repo. It will:

Ask you which issue tracker you want to use (GitHub, GitLab, local files, or anything else you describe)

Ask you what labels you apply to tickets when you triage them ( /triage uses labels)

Ask you where you want to save any docs we create

3. Bam - you're ready to go.

Why These Skills Exist

I built these skills as a way to fix common failure modes I see with Claude Code, Codex, and other coding agents.

#1: The Agent Didn't Do What I Want

"No-one knows exactly what they want"

David Thomas & Andrew Hunt, The Pragmatic Programmer

The Problem . The most common failure mode in software development is misalignment. You think the dev knows what you want. Then you see what they've built - and you realize it didn't understand you at all.

This is just the same in the AI age. There is a communication gap between you and the agent. The fix for this is a grilling session - getting the agent to ask you detailed questions about what you're building.

The Fix is to use:

/grill-me - for non-code uses

/grill-with-docs - same as /grill-me , but adds more goodies (see below)

These are my most popular skills. They help you align with the agent before you get started, and think deeply about the change you're making. Use them every time you want to make a change.

#2: The Agent Is Way Too Verbose

With a ubiquitous language, conversations among developers and expressions of the code are all derived from the same domain model.

Eric Evans, Domain-Driven-Design

The Problem : At the start of a project, devs and the people they're building the software for (the domain experts) are usually speaking different languages.

I felt the same tension with my agents. Agents are usually dropped into a project and asked to figure out the jargon as they go. So they use 20 words where 1 will do.

The Fix for this is a shared language. It's a document that helps agents decode the jargon used in the project.

Example

Here's an example glossary (still named CONTEXT.md at that pinned commit, from before the skills renamed the convention), from my course-video-manager repo. Which one is easier to read?

BEFORE : "There's a problem when a lesson inside a section of a course is made 'real' (i.e. given a spot in the file system)"

AFTER : "There's a problem with the materialization cascade"

This concision pays off session after session.

This is built into /grill-with-docs . It's a grilling session, but that helps you build a shared language with the AI, and document hard-to-explain decisions in ADR's.

It's hard to explain how powerful this is. It might be the single coolest technique in this repo. Try it, and see.

Tip
A shared language has many other benefits than reducing verbosity:

Variables, functions and files are named consistently , using

articles.body:
Website ·
Discord ·
English · 简体中文 · 繁體中文 · Italiano · 日本語 · Bahasa Indonesia · Português (Brasil)

Tiny engine, immense model. colibri runs very large open models on the
machine you already have. A mixture-of-experts model of hundreds of billions of
parameters uses only a small part of itself for each token, so colibri keeps
that part in RAM and reads the rest, the experts, from the disk when the model
asks for them. Pure C, one file per model family, no GPU required.

Thirteen engines run today. Ten are for language models: GLM-5.2/5.3 (which
also runs Mistral-Large-4 ), GLM-5.3-Flash , Inkling , Kimi K3 ,
DeepSeek V4 Flash , DeepSeek V4.1 Flash , MiMo-V2.6 Flash (and Pro),
Qwen3.8-Flash-Next , Qwen3.6 (which also runs Qwen3-Coder, the dense
Qwen3.8-27B, Flint , Muse Spark Open and LFM3-VL ) and OLMoE . One
draws pictures: Qwen-Image-2.1 . Two answer decisions: Laya and
GLiNER2.5-Decide , with a third decision model, Clef , on the Qwen3.6
engine. The language models also run from the GGUF files already published,
read as they are ( GGUF ), on the CPU, on any GPU through Vulkan
and on NVIDIA cards through CUDA. Which one for my machine

$ ./coli chat
colibri v2.1.0 · GLM-5.2 · 744B MoE · int4 · streaming CPU
✓ ready in 32s · resident 9.9 GB
› ciao!
◆ Ciao! Come posso aiutarti oggi?

colibri is free and open source. If it has earned a place on your machine, a coffee helps pay for the next engine and the next speedup.

Get started in one step

You need a computer with 8 GB of RAM at the very least (16 GB or more is
better), 22 GB free on the disk for the smallest model, and an internet
connection. A graphics card is optional.

Windows

On this page click Code , then Download ZIP , and unzip it.

Double-click START-HERE.bat in the unzipped folder. If Python is
missing, it offers to install it for you.

Linux (Ubuntu and Debian; other distributions have the same packages under
their own names)

sudo apt install git python3 build-essential
git clone https://github.com/JustVugg/colibri
cd colibri
./start-here.sh

macOS (with Homebrew )

xcode-select --install
brew install libomp git python
git clone https://github.com/JustVugg/colibri
cd colibri
./start-here.sh

You answer one question, which model, and Enter takes the recommendation. Then
the setup:

looks at your machine : RAM, free disk, CPU and GPUs;

recommends a model that fits : the part of the model that always stays in
RAM, plus a minimum cache of experts, must fit in your RAM, and the download
on your disk;

gets the engine : it builds it for your machine when a compiler is there,
otherwise it downloads the prebuilt one, which runs on the CPU and, on Linux
and Windows, on a Vulkan GPU too. It builds
for your GPU when that pays: CUDA for an NVIDIA card on Linux when the CUDA toolkit is installed,
otherwise Vulkan. On a discrete GPU it always does; on an integrated GPU,
which shares the CPU's RAM, only for the models measured faster there
(Qwen3.6, Qwen3-Coder and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next). If a package is missing it
prints the exact command to install it and carries on with the CPU; run the
setup again afterwards and it rebuilds for the GPU;

downloads the model with progress and resume: stop it whenever you like,
run it again and it continues where it stopped;

starts colibri and opens the dashboard in your browser, and prints the
addresses other apps can use:

Starting colibri
Browser: http://127.0.0.1:8000/
OpenAI base URL: http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1
Anthropic base URL: http://127.0.0.1:8000
stop: press Ctrl+C here (or close this window)

Next time , run START-HERE.bat or ./start-here.sh again: colibri starts
straight away, with no download and no build. c/coli status shows what is
installed and whether it runs, c/coli stop stops it ( c\coli.cmd status and
c\coli.cmd stop on Windows).

Options go after ./start-here.sh or START-HERE.bat :

Option

What it does

--list

every model against this machine, and why one does not fit

--model ID

install that model (the ids are in the tables below )

--yes

no questions: take the recommendation

--dir DIR

put the models on another disk (default ~/colibri-models )

--backend vulkan , cuda or cpu

choose the engine build yourself; --no-gpu is --backend cpu

--model-dir DIR

use a model you already downloaded

--reconfigure

choose another model

What each step does, in detail: docs/quickstart.md .

If something goes wrong

What you see

What to do

it stopped during the download

run the same command again: it resumes from the bytes already on disk

to use the GPU through ..., first run: <command>

run that command, then the setup again: it rebuilds for the GPU and does not download again

the ... build failed , for example Unsupported gpu architecture when the installed CUDA toolkit no longer supports the card

the setup checks the toolkit against the card first and picks Vulkan by itself, saying why; if a build still fails it offers the next one (Vulkan, then the CPU). ./start-here.sh --backend vulkan forces Vulkan

https://kornia.readthedocs.io

English | 简体中文

Docs • Try it Now • Tutorials • Examples • Blog • Community
articles.body:
English | 简体中文

Docs •
Try it Now •
Tutorials •
Examples •
Blog •
Community

Kornia is a differentiable computer vision library that provides a rich set of differentiable image processing and geometric vision algorithms. Built on top of PyTorch , Kornia integrates seamlessly into existing AI workflows, allowing you to leverage powerful batch transformations , auto-differentiation and GPU acceleration . Whether you're working on image transformations, augmentations, or AI-driven image processing, Kornia equips you with the tools you need to bring your ideas to life.

📢 Direction : Kornia is becoming the reference implementation and executable specification for differentiable computer vision and geometry in the PyTorch ecosystem — explicit conventions, conformance tests, and honest benchmarks over API growth. Read the Roadmap .

When to use Kornia

Kornia pays off where a hand-written version gets long or fragile, or where the alternatives leave the GPU:

Breadth. 1,200+ public operators, most with no torchvision equivalent: camera models and
epipolar geometry, minimal solvers and RANSAC, feature detection, description and matching, edge detection,
morphology, Lab and Bayer color, image losses and metrics. torchvision overlaps mainly on resizing, cropping,
flipping, color jitter and blur.

Per-sample parameters in one batched call. gaussian_blur2d(x, (9, 9), sigma) takes a (B, 2) sigma ;
rotate takes a (B,) angle, warp_affine / warp_perspective take (B, 2, 3) / (B, 3, 3) matrices and
adjust_brightness a (B,) factor. torchvision's functional ops apply one parameter per call. From Kornia 0.9.1,
a sigma tensor and the enhancement value checks (gamma, contrast, solarize) are validated on the device, so a
CUDA call, or an MPS call on PyTorch ≥ 2.13, needs no host synchronization for them.

Batched minimal solvers and robust estimation. find_fundamental(x1, x2, method="7POINT") solves (B, 7, 2)
samples and returns all real solutions in (B, 3, 3, 3) , with zero matrices in the unused slots; the 8-point,
5-point essential ( find_essential ), DLT homography and PnP ( solve_pnp_dlt ) solvers are there too. RANSAC
(homography, fundamental and essential models) samples and scores hypotheses on the device; by default its
refinement and final selection run on the host in float64, and compile=True (PyTorch ≥ 2.14, CPU and CUDA) runs
the whole estimation as one compiled graph on the device.

Differentiable geometry. Depth to 3D and back ( depth_to_3d_v2 , unproject_points , project_points ),
warp_frame_depth , remap , camera models with Brown–Conrady and Kannala–Brandt distortion, and Lie groups ( So3 ,
Se3 ) keep gradients with respect to depth, pose and camera parameters.

Annotated augmentation. AugmentationSequential applies one sampled transform to images, masks, boxes and
keypoints together and can invert it, in 2D; the 3D augmentations transform volumes, without annotations or an
inverse. On CUDA, augmentations move their sampled parameters to the
GPU without blocking it, and a sync-guard test keeps every public augmentation free of avoidable host
synchronizations.

Local features on the GPU. SIFT and HardNet, DISK, ALIKED, XFeat, DeDoDe, LoFTR and LightGlue, with
mutual-nearest-neighbour and ratio-test matchers.

Morphology with arbitrary structuring elements on batched tensors.

Compiles and exports. Nearly all probed operator configurations run under torch.compile and match eager,
and over 1,000 export to ONNX; the result for every operator is on the
export support page .

Fast where it is designed to be: batched tensors on a GPU. In the published 0.9.0 flagship benchmarks (RTX 4090,
batch 32), many filters, warps, feature-matching steps and image metrics run about 10× to 70× faster in eager mode
than per-image OpenCV or scikit-image on the CPU, and torch.compile takes several of them past 100×. On the small
overlap with torchvision on the same GPU, eager Kornia is slower; compiled Kornia is faster for hue, color jitter
and Gaussian blur and still slower for flips, crops and brightness. OpenCV wins single-image uint8 CPU work.
Results vary with hardware and workload; every number, win and loss is published on the
performance page .

These operators run on the input's device with no NumPy round trip, and most are differentiable; robust estimation
( RANSAC ) and the extraction methods of learned features such as DeDoDe and XFeat run without gradients. For a
single fixed-parameter operation, such as one blur or one resize, a few lines of PyTorch or torchvision are just as
good.

Key Components

Differentiable Image Processing

Kornia provides a comprehensive suite of image processing operators, all differentiable and ready to integrate into deep learning pipelines.

Filters : Gaussian, Sobel, Median, Box Blur, etc.

Transformations : Affine, Homography, Perspective, etc.

Enhancements : Histogram Equalization, CLAHE, Gamma Correction, etc.

Edge Detection : Canny, Laplacian, Sobel, etc.

... check our docs for more.

Kronos is the first open-source foundation model for financial candlesticks (K-lines),
trained on data from over 45 global exchanges .

📰 News

🚩 [2025.11.10] Kronos has been accpeted by AAAI 2026.

🚩 [2025.08.17] We have released the scripts for fine-tuning! Check them out to adapt Kronos to your own tasks.

🚩 [2025.08.02] Our paper is now available on arXiv !

📜 Introduction

Kronos is a family of decoder-only foundation models, pre-trained specifically for the "language" of financial markets—K-line sequences. Unlike general-purpose TSFMs, Kronos is designed to handle the unique, high-noise characteristics of financial data. It leverages a novel two-stage framework:

A specialized tokenizer first quantizes continuous, multi-dimensional K-line data (OHLCV) into hierarchical discrete tokens .

A large, autoregressive Transformer is then pre-trained on these tokens, enabling it to serve as a unified model for diverse quantitative tasks.

✨ Live Demo

We have set up a live demo to visualize Kronos's forecasting results. The webpage showcases a forecast for the BTC/USDT trading pair over the next 24 hours.

👉 Access the Live Demo Here

📦 Model Zoo

We release a family of pre-trained models with varying capacities to suit different computational and application needs. All models are readily accessible from the Hugging Face Hub.

🚀 Getting Started

Installation

Install Python 3.10+, and then install the dependencies:

pip install -r requirements.txt

📈 Making Forecasts

Forecasting with Kronos is straightforward using the KronosPredictor class. It handles data preprocessing, normalization, prediction, and inverse normalization, allowing you to get from raw data to forecasts in just a few lines of code.

Important Note : The max_context for Kronos-small and Kronos-base is 512 . This is the maximum sequence length the model can process. For optimal performance, it is recommended that your input data length (i.e., lookback ) does not exceed this limit. The KronosPredictor will automatically handle truncation for longer contexts.

Here is a step-by-step guide to making your first forecast.

1. Load the Tokenizer and Model

First, load a pre-trained Kronos model and its corresponding tokenizer from the Hugging Face Hub.

from model import Kronos , KronosTokenizer , KronosPredictor

# Load from Hugging Face Hub
tokenizer = KronosTokenizer . from_pretrained ( "NeoQuasar/Kronos-Tokenizer-base" )
model = Kronos . from_pretrained ( "NeoQuasar/Kronos-small" )

2. Instantiate the Predictor

Create an instance of KronosPredictor , passing the model, tokenizer, and desired device.

# Initialize the predictor
predictor = KronosPredictor ( model , tokenizer , max_context = 512 )

3. Prepare Input Data

The predict method requires three main inputs:

df : A pandas DataFrame containing the historical K-line data. It must include columns ['open', 'high', 'low', 'close'] . volume and amount are optional.

x_timestamp : A pandas Series of timestamps corresponding to the historical data in df .

y_timestamp : A pandas Series of timestamps for the future periods you want to predict.

import pandas as pd

# Load your data
df = pd . read_csv ( "./data/XSHG_5min_600977.csv" )
df [ 'timestamps' ] = pd . to_datetime ( df [ 'timestamps' ])

# Define context window and prediction length
lookback = 400
pred_len = 120

# Prepare inputs for the predictor
x_df = df . loc [: lookback - 1 , [ 'open' , 'high' , 'low' , 'close' , 'volume' , 'amount' ]]
x_timestamp = df . loc [: lookback - 1 , 'timestamps' ]
y_timestamp = df . loc [ lookback : lookback + pred_len - 1 , 'timestamps' ]

4. Generate Forecasts

Call the predict method to generate forecasts. You can control the sampling process with parameters like T , top_p , and sample_count for probabilistic forecasting.

# Generate predictions
pred_df = predictor . predict (
df = x_df ,
x_timestamp = x_timestamp ,
y_timestamp = y_timestamp ,
pred_len = pred_len ,
T = 1.0 , # Temperature for sampling
top_p = 0.9 , # Nucleus sampling probability
sample_count = 1 # Number of forecast paths to generate and average
)

print ( "Forecasted Data Head:" )
print ( pred_df . head ())

The predict method returns a pandas DataFrame containing the forecasted values for open , high , low , close , volume , and amount , indexed by the y_timestamp you provided.

nix profile add github:NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-unstable#t3code

articles.body:
| Download | Paper | Developer Slack | Community Discord | Community WeChat |

Unlock datacenter-class intelligence on the hardware you already own — Run 290B+ frontier MoE models locally on your gaming PC at blistering interactive speeds.

About

FreeToken is an edge-native Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) serving engine designed for running frontier-scale open-weight models on personal and consumer hardware. It treats heterogeneous edge resources—GPUs, CPUs, host memory, and interconnects—as a unified, elastic inference platform. Its core features include:

Fast Edge-Native Runtime : Provides efficient MoE serving with bandwidth-adaptive CPU–GPU co-execution ( $q^\star$ policy), full-layer double-buffered prefill streaming, global LRU expert caching, graph-compatible execution, and the FTW fast weight format.

Semantic-Aware Caching : Features semantic anchor checkpoints for recurrent state and KV caches, allowing agentic context edits (e.g., tool calls, thinking blocks) to avoid redundant context recomputation.

Elastic Memory Management : Supports dynamic, runtime VRAM re-allocation between expert caches and KV memory without engine restarts or weight reloading.

Broad MoE & Ecosystem Support : Supports frontier open-weight MoE models (e.g., DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, GLM-5.2) across various parameter scales and quantization formats (e.g., MXFP4, NVFP4, FP8, BF16), with Anthropic/OpenAI-compatible APIs for seamless integration with real-world coding and tool-calling agents (e.g., Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenClaw, DeepSeek Harness).

Diverse Consumer Hardware : Scales across consumer laptops, gaming desktops, and workstation GPUs, with native support for NVIDIA RTX 30, RTX 40, and RTX 50 series GPUs.

Getting Started

Desktop app

Download FreeToken for Windows or Linux at flashml.ai . It sets the engine up for you and gives you a GUI for running models, chatting, and tuning the engine.

uv pip install " freetoken[accel] "

Or build from source:

git clone https://github.com/FlashML-org/FreeToken.git && cd FreeToken

Claude Code Game Studios

Turn a single Claude Code session into a full game development studio.

Why This Exists

Building a game solo with AI is powerful — but a single chat session has no structure. No one stops you from hardcoding magic numbers, skipping design docs, or writing spaghetti code. There's no QA pass, no design review, no one asking "does this actually fit the game's vision?"

Claude Code Game Studios solves this by giving your AI session the structure of a real studio. from scrapling . fetchers import Fetcher

from scrapling . spiders import Spider , Response

class QuotesSpider ( Spider ):
name = "quotes"
start_urls = [ "https://quotes.toscrape.com/" ]

}

Grok Bot already re-reads the log from disk. This does not write profile.md , user-memory, or project memory. Disable with CLAUDE_MEM_GROK_BOT_AWARENESS_ENABLED=false .

Install with a single command:

npx claude-mem install

The installer sets everything up first, then asks you to sign in to claude-mem in your browser (email magic link — no card required). When the free trial ends, memory automatically falls back to your Anthropic plan unless you subscribe. After sign-in you pick your memory provider — the claude-mem observer, your own OpenRouter or Gemini key, or your Anthropic plan.

Prefer to skip the sign-in? Pass an explicit --provider flag, set CLAUDE_MEM_ONLINE_OPTIN=false , or run in CI/non-interactive shells — the installer completes without any account interaction.

Or install for OpenCode:

This works with OpenCode 1.3.4 or later, including OpenCode 2. Restart OpenCode after installing.

Or install for T3 Code (Codex and Claude Code providers):

The installer discovers T3 Code's enabled providers, registers native Claude-Mem plugins in their configured homes, and supports T3-managed Codex. Restart T3 Code, trust the provider's hooks when prompted, and start a new thread. See the T3 Code integration guide for custom server settings, status, and removal.

Or install for Antigravity CLI ( setup guide ):

Or install for OMP (Oh My Pi):

Or install the native Pi extension or DeepSeek Harness plugin:

npx claude-mem install --ide dsh --dsh-profile tui

Pi and DeepSeek Harness use the worker runtime. See native harness setup for capture, recall, and troubleshooting.

Or install from the plugin marketplace inside Claude Code:

/plugin install claude-mem

Restart Claude Code. Context from previous sessions will automatically appear in new sessions.

Note: Claude-Mem is also published on npm, but npm install -g claude-mem installs the SDK/library only — it does not register the plugin hooks or set up the worker service. Always install via npx claude-mem install or the /plugin commands above.

articles.body:
agent-desktop

Computer use for AI agents: see and operate desktop apps on macOS, Windows, and Linux through the OS accessibility tree.

agent-desktop gives an AI agent computer use without screenshots or pixel matching. It reads the accessibility tree of a desktop app and returns it as JSON, with a ref for every element the agent can act on. The agent clicks or types on a ref, reads the UI again to check the result, and repeats. The loop lives in your agent; agent-desktop has no model inside. It ships as a CLI and a C library.

Snapshots, clipboard reads, screenshots, command output, and debug artifacts can contain private desktop content. Keep them out of public logs and uploads.

Install

npm install -g agent-desktop
agent-desktop status # platform, permissions, supported surfaces
agent-desktop permissions --guide # macOS: walks you through the Accessibility grant

Bun, Yarn and pnpm can install the same package. It includes native binaries and platform helpers for x64 and ARM64.
For direct execution without a JavaScript launcher, download the matching native archive from
GitHub Releases and keep its helper beside the executable.

On macOS and Linux, Homebrew also works: brew install agent-desktop . There is no official Scoop package yet.
The repository no longer maintains a custom Homebrew tap or Scoop bucket.

Release archives and building from source are covered in Installation .

Quick start

agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i # interactive elements, each with a ref
agent-desktop click @s8f3k2p9:e8 # act on a ref from that snapshot
agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i # observe again to verify

Each command prints one JSON envelope. A trimmed snapshot:

{
"version" : " 2.6 " ,
"ok" : true ,
"command" : " snapshot " ,
"data" : {
"app" : " Finder " ,
"snapshot_id" : " s8f3k2p9 " ,
"ref_count" : 59 ,
"complete" : true ,
"tree" : {
"role" : " window " ,
"name" : " Downloads " ,
"children" : [
{ "role" : " treeitem " , "name" : " Documents " , "ref_id" : " @s8f3k2p9:e8 " , "available_actions" : [ " Click " ] }
]
}
}
}

Refs carry their snapshot id. A bare @e8 fails with INVALID_ARGS .

If the UI changed, an action returns STALE_REF or AMBIGUOUS_TARGET . Take a new snapshot and use its refs.

Actions are headless by default: no pointer movement, no focus change. Pass --headed for physical input.

In PowerShell, quote every ref ( '@s8f3k2p9:e8' ), because a bare @token is the splatting operator.

The full walkthrough is in the quick start .

How it works

Your agent calls the CLI, or the C library in process. Both run the same core, which reaches the OS only through PlatformAdapter . Each binary is built for one OS and talks to that OS's accessibility API.

For AI agents

The binary carries guides that match its version:

agent-desktop skills get desktop # the loop, refs, verification and retry rules
agent-desktop skills get platform # what differs on the OS you run on
agent-desktop < command > --help # flags for one command

Install the skill into an agent harness from skills.sh :

npx skills add https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-desktop --skill agent-desktop

Or add this to your AGENTS.md :

Use ` agent-desktop ` to see and operate desktop apps. Before the first use, run
` agent-desktop skills get desktop ` and ` agent-desktop skills get platform ` , and follow them.

Retry a failed command only when error.disposition.retry is safe . See JSON output for the envelope, error codes, and exit codes.

MCP

agent-desktop mcp serves every command as an MCP tool over stdio. A tool is named after its command ( desktop_snapshot , desktop_click , desktop_session_start ), takes that command's arguments, and returns its JSON envelope:

{ "mcpServers" : { "agent-desktop" : { "command" : " agent-desktop " , "args" : [ " mcp " ] } } }

Global flags given to mcp , such as --session , --headed or --trace , apply to every call.

Commands

agent-desktop has 60 command names, 56 operational commands. The other four ( key-down , key-up , mouse-down , mouse-up ) refuse to run until a daemon can release a held key or button. Commands documents each one.

Group

Commands

Observe

snapshot , find , get , is , screenshot , list-surfaces

Act on a ref

click , double-click , triple-click , right-click , type , set-value , clear , focus , select , toggle , check , uncheck , expand , collapse , scroll , scroll-to

Keyboard and mouse

press , hover , drag , mouse-move , mouse-click , mouse-wheel , key-down , key-up , mouse-down , mouse-up

Apps and windows

launch , close-app , list-apps , list-windows , list-displays , focus-window , resize-window , move-window , minimize , maximize , restore , open-system-surface

Notifications

list-notifications , dismiss-notification , dismiss-all-notifications , notification-action

Clipboard

clipboard-get , clipboard-set , clipboard-clear

Wait

wait

Sessions

session , trace , cursor-overlay

System

status , permissions , version , batch , skills

Platform support
